# 41. Organization, venue and event branding

## 41.1 Branding is a platform capability

The application MUST support an organization-specific visual identity. A deployment configured for GHB should look and behave as a GHB-branded system in the authorized administration shell, staff workspaces, Guest Portal and generated materials. A second organization using the same software must be able to use its own identity without affecting GHB.

Branding is attached to the organization/tenant and optionally overridden by a venue or event. It is not tied to an individual staff account. Individual users may choose accessibility or interface preferences (for example, light/dark mode), but those preferences MUST NOT change the organization’s invitations, passes, reports or public presentation.

## 41.2 Inheritance and precedence

Brand resolution uses this precedence:

`Event override -> Venue brand profile -> Organization brand profile -> Platform default`

Each layer may override selected properties rather than requiring a complete brand definition. Missing values inherit from the next level. The resolved brand is materialized as a versioned snapshot when an event template or generated artifact is published.

Examples:

- Organization: GHB logo, primary colours, typography, graphic style and default templates.
- Venue: optional venue-specific location mark, room motif or venue-specific directions/signage.
- Event: optional anniversary/conference sub-brand, event title graphic, special accent or event-specific image.

A venue or event override MUST NOT mutate the underlying organization profile. Authorized users can preview the resolved brand before publication.

## 41.3 Brand profile contents

A brand profile should support:

- Primary, secondary, accent, neutral and status colour tokens.
- Light-background and dark-background logo variants (SVG/PNG, with safe sanitization).
- Optional wordmark, emblem, seal, sponsor marks and partner logos with display rules.
- Typography choices and approved fallback fonts.
- Header/footer treatments, backgrounds, patterns and image assets.
- Icon/illustration style and optional venue/event graphics.
- Document margins, visual hierarchy and template-specific display rules.
- Language-specific organization name, address, contact and footer text.
- Optional display name and sender identity metadata for approved communication channels.

Brand assets are uploaded to private, tenant-scoped storage, validated for file type/size and referenced by immutable asset IDs. SVG assets must be sanitized before use. The system must not load arbitrary remote assets into sensitive interfaces or documents.

## 41.4 Surfaces that inherit the brand

The resolved brand may apply to:

- Login/organization selection and authorized application shell.
- Admin Cockpit and staff workspaces.
- Guest Portal and event landing page.
- Digital invitations, RSVP pages and confirmation messages.
- Guest cards, badges and admission passes.
- QR-code framing and credential print layouts (the token itself remains opaque).
- Seating plans, venue maps, zone legends and wayfinding sheets.
- Reception signage and coordinator printouts.
- Reports, exports and event summary PDFs.
- Approved email templates and other configured communication channels.

Branding must never override information classification. A restricted attachment or internal-only note must not become guest-visible because it is placed in a branded template.

## 41.5 Templates and revision control

Templates are scoped to organization, venue or event and have their own revisions. A generated invitation, card or report records the template revision and resolved brand revision used. A later brand change MUST NOT silently alter previously generated or distributed material. Reissue/re-render is an explicit operation.

Template categories include invitation, RSVP, guest card, QR pass, seating plan, zone plan, wayfinding sheet, check-in sign, report and operational summary. Templates support field bindings to approved data, conditional blocks, language variants, print dimensions and preview data. Template editing is permission-controlled and changes are previewed before publishing.

## 41.6 Multi-tenant and deployment model

The initial GHB deployment may run as a single-organization installation. The data model MUST remain tenant-aware: every organization-owned entity carries an organization/tenant scope, and every query/write is validated against that scope. A shared multi-organization deployment may be enabled later only after tenant isolation tests, storage isolation and permission review pass.

Organization branding, assets, templates, Guest Registry people and venue templates are isolated by tenant. A user belonging to multiple organizations selects an active organization context; the server validates this context for each request. A venue belongs to an organization, while an event may reference one or more venues belonging to the same organization or to explicitly authorized partner organizations.

## 41.7 Acceptance criteria

- GHB branding appears consistently across the configured application, portal, invitations, passes and print templates.
- A second organization can use a different logo, palette and templates without cross-contamination.
- Venue and event overrides can change selected tokens while inheriting the rest.
- A published artifact retains the exact brand/template revisions used to generate it.
- Rebranding does not silently modify already-issued passes or sent invitations.
- Brand asset URLs and template records cannot be accessed across tenant boundaries.

# 42. GHB reference venue portfolio

## 42.1 Reference deployment, not a hardcoded product assumption

Gazi Husrev-beg’s Library (GHB) is the first reference organization/tenant for discovery and initial configuration. The platform remains a general-purpose product. GHB names, brand assets, room names, capacities and layouts must be stored as organization data and venue templates, not embedded as application constants.

The initial GHB reference portfolio should include:

- Large hall.
- Medium hall.
- Small hall.
- Mosque/prayer-space configuration used for selected events or event sessions.

The mosque/prayer space may be registered as a separate venue/site or as a related space under the GHB organization, depending on the actual operational and ownership structure. The software must not assume that it is physically part of the Library building. The hierarchy can represent a venue portfolio with distinct sites.

## 42.2 Reusable space templates

Each hall or space has a versioned template containing:

- Physical/site identity and hierarchy.
- Floor-plan background and calibration.
- Room boundary and usable areas.
- Zones and their visual styles.
- Spatial features and non-allocatable regions.
- Tables, fixed seats, rows, floor-position resources or capacity pools.
- Approved capacities and source/approval metadata.
- Entrances and public/staff navigation points.
- Layer visibility and audience projections.
- Default allocation model and numbering scheme.

An event session references an immutable venue-template revision. Changes to a master template do not silently change an event already in planning, approved or live.

## 42.3 Supplied mosque seating workbook - observed reference

The supplied workbook, `plan begove džamije menšura.xlsx`, contains one worksheet and a cell-formatted visual plan. It is a practical reference for the way the venue is currently organized. The workbook is not a relational guest list and should not be treated as a direct source of live guest allocations.

The visible plan includes the following annotations (all values require confirmation by the venue coordinator before becoming authoritative system capacity values):

| Workbook annotation | What the platform should represent |
|---|---|
| CRVENA ZONA = 74 | Red zone polygon/region with a proposed capacity annotation of 74. |
| ZELENA ZONA = 150 | Green zone polygon/region with a proposed capacity annotation of 150. |
| PLAVA ZONA = 140 | Blue zone polygon/region with a proposed capacity annotation of 140. |
| MAHFIL DONJI = 14 | Named special area with a proposed capacity annotation of 14. |
| MAHFIL GORNJI = 10 | Named special area with a proposed capacity annotation of 10. |
| MAKSURA LIJEVA = 10 | Named left-side special area with a proposed capacity annotation of 10. |
| MAKSURA DESNA = 10 | Named right-side special area with a proposed capacity annotation of 10. |

The drawing also labels or depicts a minber, pillars (`STUB`), a passage (`STUB I PROLAZ`), an entrance (`ULAZ`) and footwear areas (`OBUĆA`), alongside numbered blocks/rows. These are important venue features and must be represented as their correct spatial types rather than being interpreted as seats.

## 42.4 Numbering and labels

The workbook shows visible numbering sequences repeated in different blocks/rows/areas. The same display number can occur in more than one place. Therefore:

- A display number is not a globally unique identifier.
- Each place receives an immutable internal resource ID.
- The visible locator is composed from its parents, such as `BLUE / ROW 04 / POSITION 12` or `MAHFIL DONJI / POSITION 03`.
- Numbering schemes are configurable by zone, row, block or special area.
- The interface and exports must make the scope explicit so two different “Seat 1” or “Position 1” labels are never ambiguous.

## 42.5 Capacity confirmation

The annotated numbers in the workbook are source values, not automatically approved occupancy limits. Before activation, an authorized venue representative must confirm:

- Whether each annotation is a seat/position count, a recommended allocation limit or another planning figure.
- Whether the named special areas overlap or are included in the coloured-zone values.
- Which spaces are allocatable, reserved or non-allocatable.
- Whether a row/position is suitable for individual assignment or should remain zone-only.
- The operational limit to use for each event configuration.

Do not sum overlapping annotations or calculate a total capacity until their relationship is confirmed.

# 43. Generalized spatial allocation model

## 43.1 Four separate concepts

The v1.2 spatial model distinguishes four concepts that must not be collapsed into a single “seat” table:

1. **Spatial feature:** a physical object or landmark, such as a pillar, wall, minber, entrance, footwear area, passage or stage. Usually not assignable.
2. **Spatial region:** a polygon or boundary, such as a room, coloured zone, reserved area or no-allocation area.
3. **Allocation resource:** an individually assignable unit, such as a chair, numbered theatre seat, floor position, desk position or row segment.
4. **Capacity pool:** a quantity limit for an area where individual positions are not assigned, such as general admission or a zone-only allocation.

A visual object can exist without an allocation resource. A capacity pool can exist without individually drawn positions.

## 43.2 Allocation modes

A space can enable one or more modes:

- `individual_seat`: one guest per physical chair/seat.
- `numbered_floor_position`: one guest per logical position on a floor/carpet, with no chair implied.
- `row_or_segment`: assign a guest/group to a row or bounded segment without choosing a precise position.
- `zone_capacity`: assign a guest/group to a zone and decrement its approved capacity.
- `unassigned_open`: no individual placement; attendance is counted at a broader level, subject to event policy.

The allocation engine must know which mode applies to each resource/space. It must not invent seat objects in a zone-only layout.

## 43.3 Numbering scopes

Each resource may have a visible label and a numbering scheme. Numbering scope can be:

- Venue-wide.
- Space/room-wide.
- Zone-wide.
- Section/block-wide.
- Row-wide.
- Parent resource-specific (for example, seat numbers within a table).

The internal resource ID remains globally unique within the tenant. The composed locator is generated from the hierarchy and can be localized/formatted for cards, portal and printouts.

## 43.4 Spatial geometry and operational features

The native editor should support:

- Points for individual positions, entrances and landmarks.
- Lines/poly-lines for rows, aisles, paths and boundaries.
- Polygons for rooms, zones, reserved areas, special areas and restricted regions.
- Rotated rectangles/circles/custom shapes for furniture and obstacles.
- Layers and audience-specific visibility.

The map must support explicit orientation, labels, a legend and accessible non-colour identifiers. Colour coding is useful but MUST NOT be the only way to distinguish a zone; every zone also needs a name/code/pattern or other readable identifier.

## 43.5 Position allocation and group placement

For a prayer-row layout, an administrator may allocate:

- A guest to a zone only.
- A guest to a zone and row.
- A guest to a specific numbered floor position.
- A family/delegation to a contiguous range or group of positions, where supported by rules and capacity.

The engine should preserve contiguous group placements when requested, support explicit separation across zones/rows, and report when a group cannot fit within the available contiguous capacity. It must not assume that a row's positions are physically identical to cinema seats; the spatial resource type carries the distinction.

## 43.6 Capacity validation

The capacity model supports both explicit resource counts and manually approved zone limits. The system may display counts derived from configured resources, but an authorized venue representative must approve the operational limit. The strictest applicable approved limit is used. The editor must show the source and approval date for capacity values.

# 44. Spreadsheet floor-plan onboarding

## 44.1 Treat the workbook as a reference artifact

The supplied Excel map is a cell-formatted drawing with grid boundaries, labels, colours and visible numbering. It is not a structured GIS/CAD object model and it is not a guest allocation database. The application must preserve the original workbook as an immutable source artifact and must not assume that every cell containing a number represents an independently assignable place.

## 44.2 Import workflow

1. Upload the original XLSX into a private source-artifact store and calculate a content hash.
2. Select worksheet(s) and import the workbook as a read-only reference.
3. Render the selected sheet to PDF/image using a controlled server-side conversion process; preserve the original workbook unchanged.
4. Display the rendered plan in the native floor-plan editor as a locked background layer.
5. Set orientation, crop, scale and a known measurement where available.
6. Trace/define room boundaries, coloured zones, special areas and non-allocatable features.
7. Create rows, row segments and optional numbered floor-position resources; import readable labels/numbers as suggestions where extraction is reliable.
8. Map source regions/labels to native spatial objects, retaining the source worksheet and cell/region references where feasible.
9. Validate numbering scopes, duplicate display labels, capacities, overlaps, entrances, passages and no-allocation areas.
10. Compare the native reconstruction side-by-side with the source workbook and have an authorized venue coordinator review it.
11. Approve and version the native venue template; record approver, date, source hash and any assumptions.

## 44.3 Automation boundaries

The application MAY extract text, cell values, merged ranges, formatting, borders and fill colours to assist the conversion. Such extraction is advisory. It MUST NOT infer that every numeric cell is a seat, that each colour is a capacity zone, or that numeric annotations are validated capacities without review. The initial release should prioritize a reliable reference-background-plus-trace workflow over fragile automatic reconstruction of arbitrary Excel artwork.

## 44.4 Source-to-native traceability

Each native object created from the source plan may carry a source reference: workbook hash, worksheet name, source cell/range or visual region, extraction method and reviewer. When the native plan changes, the source remains immutable and can be reopened for comparison. A future revision may be imported as a new source artifact and compared against the current native plan.

## 44.5 Conversion acceptance criteria

- The original workbook is retained and downloadable only by authorized venue/floor-plan users.
- The source is rendered consistently for visual comparison.
- The editor can overlay editable zones, spatial features and positions.
- Repeated display numbers are accepted when their parent scopes differ.
- Duplicate internal resource IDs are impossible.
- Position and capacity counts are reviewed before approval.
- The approved native plan can be published to staff and a sanitized guest-visible projection can be generated separately.

# 45. External prerequisites and CDI coordination

Section 15 is the authoritative functional definition. This section records the v1.2 boundary for data, API, cockpit and acceptance design.

## 45.1 Data and API

Use an `event_prerequisites` record with fields such as `event_id`, `prerequisite_type`, `display_label`, `required`, `readiness_gate`, `external_party_name/reference`, `internal_owner_user_id`, `status`, `request_submitted_at`, `external_reference`, `scheduled_at`, `completion_recorded_at`, `completion_recorded_by`, `completion_reference`, `notes` and timestamps. Keep a `prerequisite_status_history` table for transitions. Optional supporting documents must use restricted storage and retention.

Representative routes:

- `GET /api/v1/events/{eventId}/prerequisites`
- `POST /api/v1/events/{eventId}/prerequisites`
- `PATCH /api/v1/prerequisites/{prerequisiteId}`
- `POST /api/v1/prerequisites/{prerequisiteId}/record-completion`
- `GET /api/v1/prerequisites/{prerequisiteId}/history`

These are illustrative route names, not final OpenAPI definitions.

## 45.2 Cockpit integration

The Cockpit may show the prerequisite label, required/not-required state, current coordination status, due date and internal owner. It must not expose inspection methods, confidential correspondence or external authority reports to general event staff. A readiness gate is a workflow rule configured by the organization, not an independent legal determination by the software.

## 45.3 Acceptance criteria

- An administrator can mark CDI as required or not required and record who made the decision.
- An internal coordinator can record request submission, reference, scheduled time and completion confirmation.
- Status changes are timestamped and auditable.
- If configured as a required gate, the event cannot enter the configured Ready state until completion is recorded or an authorized exception is applied.
- The interface clearly states that the police perform the inspection.
- No internal inspection checklist, findings-management or inspection-methodology feature is implemented.

# 46. v1.2 data, API, security, delivery and acceptance updates

## 46.1 Data-model additions and refinements

Add or formalize:

- `brand_profiles`, `brand_profile_revisions`, `brand_assets`, `brand_template_assignments`, `venue_brand_overrides`, `event_brand_overrides`, `event_brand_snapshots`.
- `source_plan_artifacts`, `source_plan_mappings`, `spatial_features`, `spatial_regions`, `spatial_rows`/`row_segments` and typed `allocation_resources` for chairs, floor positions and capacity pools.
- `event_prerequisites`, `external_parties` and `prerequisite_status_history`.
- Tenant/organization scope on brand assets, templates, venue templates, Guest Registry records and generated documents.

The physical schema must preserve the four-way distinction between a non-allocatable spatial feature, a spatial region, an assignable resource and a capacity pool.

## 46.2 API surface additions

In addition to the endpoint families in Section 19, provide:

| Domain | Illustrative endpoints |
|---|---|
| Organization brand | `GET/PATCH /api/v1/organizations/{organizationId}/brand-profile` |
| Brand assets | `POST /api/v1/organizations/{organizationId}/brand-assets`, `GET/DELETE /api/v1/brand-assets/{assetId}` |
| Venue brand | `GET/PATCH /api/v1/venues/{venueId}/brand-profile` |
| Event brand override | `GET/PATCH /api/v1/events/{eventId}/brand-override` |
| Template revisions | `POST /api/v1/templates/{templateId}/revisions`, `POST /api/v1/templates/{templateId}/publish` |
| Source plan | `POST /api/v1/rooms/{roomId}/source-plan-artifacts`, `POST /api/v1/source-plans/{artifactId}/conversion-jobs` |
| Native spatial objects | `GET/POST /api/v1/floorplans/{revisionId}/spatial-objects`, `PATCH /api/v1/spatial-objects/{objectId}` |
| Floor-position resources | `GET/POST /api/v1/rooms/{roomId}/resources` with typed resource payloads |
| External prerequisites | `GET/POST /api/v1/events/{eventId}/prerequisites`, `PATCH /api/v1/prerequisites/{prerequisiteId}`, `POST /api/v1/prerequisites/{prerequisiteId}/record-completion` |

Every endpoint validates tenant, event and venue scope server-side. A brand profile or template cannot be fetched using an ID belonging to another tenant.

## 46.3 Security and privacy

- Tenant isolation applies to API queries, database relations, file storage, cache keys, WebSocket subscriptions, jobs and exports.
- Brand assets and templates are tenant-scoped; public asset delivery is allowed only for assets explicitly published for a guest-facing surface.
- Event/venue map projections remain audience-specific. A branded map is not automatically a public map.
- Guest-facing outputs expose only approved names/locators and approved map layers.
- Source workbooks may contain internal venue geometry; they are not public assets by default.
- Prerequisite records contain coordination metadata only; optional documents are separately classified and access-audited.
- Any organization-shared deployment must pass cross-tenant access tests before use with multiple organizations.

## 46.4 Revised implementation sequence

**Phase 0 - GHB discovery and reference-plan validation**

- Confirm GHB organization/tenant naming and brand assets.
- Inventory large, medium and small halls and the mosque/prayer-space relationship.
- Confirm physical hierarchy and ownership/management boundaries.
- Validate the supplied workbook's zone names, annotated capacities, position numbering, special areas, entrances and non-allocatable features with venue representatives.
- Decide which mosque areas require zone-only, row-only or numbered floor-position allocation.
- Agree whether CDI is a readiness gate for relevant event profiles and who records completion.

**Phase 1 - Multi-tenant/organization foundation and branding**

- Organization, user and permission model with tenant scope.
- Brand profiles, asset library, inheritance, revisions and basic branded app shell.
- Venue registry and versioned venue templates.
- Guest Registry and event participation model.

**Phase 2 - Spatial editor and allocation foundation**

- PDF/image/XLSX source artifact onboarding.
- Native room/zone/feature/row/resource model.
- Table, fixed-seat, capacity-zone and numbered floor-position modes.
- GHB large/medium/small hall templates and reviewed mosque template.
- Manual/hybrid allocation, constraints and solver preview.

**Phase 3 - Plans, documents, portal and staff operations**

- Branded invitations, guest cards, QR credentials and reports.
- Plan approval, publication, staff viewers and print outputs.
- Guest Portal with guest-safe map projection and venue-type-aware locator.
- Check-in, Cockpit panels, alerts and realtime updates.

**Phase 4 - Event-day coordination and resilience**

- Dynamic reflow and change notifications.
- External prerequisite coordination including CDI.
- Offline check-in, backups, restore rehearsal, monitoring and production hardening.

## 46.5 Revised production acceptance criteria

- A GHB organization profile can be configured with logo, palette, graphics, typography and templates.
- A venue/event can inherit the organization brand or override selected properties.
- Brand revisions used by invitations/cards/reports are recorded and reproducible.
- The four GHB reference spaces can be configured without hardcoded GHB-specific code.
- The mosque plan can represent red/green/blue zones, special areas, rows, numbered floor positions, pillars, minber, entrance, footwear area and passages as separate spatial objects.
- Repeated visible position numbers in different rows/zones do not collide because internal IDs and parent scopes are distinct.
- A guest can be allocated at zone, row or exact floor-position precision according to event policy.
- A tableless prayer-row layout can be allocated without creating chair records.
- The source Excel workbook remains available for comparison; native objects can be traced back to source cells/regions where feasible.
- Annotated capacities are not treated as approved until a venue representative confirms them.
- CDI can be represented as an external prerequisite, with request/schedule/completion tracking and an optional readiness gate, without implementing internal inspection activities.
- Tenant branding, files, templates, guest profiles and venue assets cannot leak between organizations.

## 46.6 Decisions confirmed for v1.2

These are the decisions now incorporated into the v1.2 baseline; operational details that require venue confirmation remain explicitly marked for Phase 0.

| Decision | v1.2 position |
|---|---|
| Branding | Organization brand is the default; venue and event overrides are supported; generated artifacts pin the resolved brand revision. |
| GHB | First reference organization/tenant and configuration dataset, not a hardcoded application branch. |
| Venue portfolio | Large, medium and small halls plus a separately modelled mosque/prayer space; physical hierarchy to be validated. |
| Mosque allocation | Coloured zones, special areas, rows/segments and optional numbered floor positions; zone-only allocation remains available. |
| Excel plan | Immutable source artifact, rendered reference background and assisted native tracing/validation; no blind automatic conversion. |
| CDI | Externally performed by police; application records coordination and completion status only. |
| Capacity | Workbook annotations are provisional until venue-approved. |
| Tenant deployment | Single-organization GHB installation is acceptable initially; schema and access model remain tenant-aware for future shared deployment. |

# Appendix H - GHB reference-plan interpretation notes

This appendix records what was read from the supplied workbook for product discovery, not a certified venue plan. The single worksheet shows an arrangement drawn with spreadsheet grid structure, borders, colour fills and labels. The visible colour zones and capacity annotations are red 74, green 150 and blue 140. It also labels mahfil lower/upper and left/right maksura areas with numerical annotations, and marks physical/navigation features such as minber, pillars, passage, entrance and footwear area. Numbered sequences repeat in separate rows/blocks. All terms, counts and geometry must be confirmed with the venue before the native template is approved.

The workbook is best treated as a **source drawing**. The production system should convert it into a layered native model with spatial regions, non-allocatable features, row/segment objects and optional numbered floor positions. It should not simply convert every spreadsheet cell or number into a seat.

# Appendix I - Branding inheritance example

The following illustrates how organization identity is inherited and selectively overridden for a venue or event.

```text
PLATFORM DEFAULT
  └── ORGANIZATION / TENANT: GHB
       ├── GHB logo, palette, typography and graphic library
       ├── GHB invitation / guest-card / report templates
       │
       ├── VENUE: LARGE HALL
       │    └── Optional venue-specific directions or mark
       ├── VENUE: MEDIUM HALL
       ├── VENUE: SMALL HALL
       └── VENUE / SPACE: MOSQUE
            └── Optional location-specific zone map theme

EVENT: Conference / Gala / Ceremony
  └── Optional event-specific campaign graphic or accent
      (inherits all unspecified properties)
```

The brand resolver produces a versioned brand snapshot used by every generated artifact. User-specific display preferences are separate from organization-facing brand identity.

# ADR 0001: Use an API-first modular monolith

- **Status:** Accepted as the initial design direction
- **Date:** 2026-11-10

## Context

Eventor spans bookings, guest management, invitations, spatial allocation, check-in and event operations. These domains are related and require consistent transactions, auditability and coordinated workflow changes. The first deployment is self-hosted and the project should remain operable without a large distributed-systems footprint.

## Decision

Build an API-first modular monolith with explicit domain/application boundaries. Use Vue 3 + TypeScript + Vite for frontends, Fastify + TypeScript for the API/workers, and PostgreSQL for authoritative data. Independently deployable UI entry points and a separate C++ optimization process are allowed where justified, but domain modules are not microservices.

## Alternatives considered

- Microservices from the outset: rejected due to operational complexity and unnecessary distributed consistency boundaries.
- Single tightly coupled application: rejected because explicit module boundaries and shared contracts are needed for long-term maintainability.

## Consequences

- Cross-domain workflows can use database transactions and shared audit conventions.
- Modules must maintain clear interfaces and avoid uncontrolled cross-module table access.
- Extracting a service later remains possible if measured operational or scaling needs justify it.

# ADR 0002: Self-hosted deployment without mandatory container or cloud dependencies

- **Status:** Accepted as the initial deployment constraint
- **Date:** 2026-11-10

## Context

The target environment is organization-controlled Linux infrastructure. The platform should remain usable without a cloud subscription and should not force Docker or a managed external service into the deployment.

## Decision

Design for self-hosted Linux deployment. Native service management (for example systemd) and a reverse proxy are valid deployment mechanisms. Containers may be offered as an optional packaging/deployment convenience, not as a mandatory runtime architecture. Do not require a cloud service, Redis/Valkey or Docker without a future ADR and explicit operational justification.

## Consequences

- Deployment, upgrades, backup and restore must be documented for the supported self-hosted path.
- Background jobs and realtime delivery need clear local infrastructure requirements.
- Optional container support must not become the only tested or documented deployment route.

# ADR 0003: Solver output is a proposal, never an automatic commit

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-10

## Context

Seating and spatial allocation can affect safety, accessibility, protocol and guest experience. Constraints may conflict or source venue plans may be incomplete. An optimizer can produce useful proposals but cannot be trusted to silently alter operational assignments.

## Decision

The allocation engine returns a proposal with feasibility status, diagnostics and objective information. The application presents a preview/diff and requires an authorized human to explicitly commit the result. Locked assignments and scoped reruns are supported. Infeasible and feasible/optimal outcomes are distinguished.

## Consequences

- Solver output is not authoritative until validated and committed through the API.
- The UI must explain conflicts and proposed changes.
- Allocation commits are auditable and concurrency-checked against the state used to generate the proposal.

# ADR 0004: Event operations are optional and responsibility-scoped

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-10
- **Related:** [Issue #8](https://github.com/TeraflopsBH/eventor/issues/8)

## Context

Eventor serves more than one organizational operating model. A venue provider (for example, GHB when renting a hall to an independent conference organizer) may only need to receive and process inquiries, reserve spaces/resources, issue offers, confirm bookings and prepare the venue. The renter is ordinarily responsible for organizing the event itself.

A venue-provider deployment should not be forced to collect guest lists, issue invitations, operate RSVP, assign guests to seats, scan admission QR codes, manage organizer-side protocols or run a full event-day cockpit simply because a customer booked a venue.

The product must also support organizations that are themselves event organizers, as well as cases where venue and organizer explicitly share or delegate operational work.

Implementation Design v0.2 already establishes an important foundation: a confirmed venue booking is not automatically an operational event, and conversion is optional. This ADR makes the operating-scope distinction explicit across the product.

## Decision

### 1. Separate venue booking from event organization

Keep these concepts distinct, even when the same legal entity performs more than one role:

- **Venue provider:** makes the venue and its own resources/services available.
- **Booking customer/requester:** submits or manages the booking inquiry.
- **Contracting party:** entity that enters into the venue agreement and may be responsible for payment.
- **Event organizer:** entity actually organizing the event.
- **Operational operator:** party or parties performing specific event tasks.

Do not assume these roles are the same organization or person. A booking-only record may exist without an Eventor operational-event record.

### 2. Operating profiles are defaults, not rigid product tiers

Each organization has a configurable default operating profile:

- **Venue provider:** booking and venue-side service delivery are the default scope.
- **Event organizer:** event planning and operational modules may be enabled by default.
- **Hybrid:** the organization may operate as venue provider for some bookings and event organizer for others.

Profiles are configuration presets, not subscription or product tiers. An event/booking can override the organization's defaults.

### 3. Activate operational modules only when needed

Operational capabilities are independently enabled within the applicable event scope. Examples include:

- Guest registry linkage and event participation.
- Invitations and RSVP.
- Seating, spatial allocation and guest wayfinding.
- Admission credentials and check-in.
- External prerequisites and organizer coordination checklists.
- Event-day cockpit, staff workspaces, alerts and timeline.
- Event communications, reports and operational documents.

No unrelated module becomes mandatory merely because another is active. Module dependencies must be explicit and minimal. For example, RSVP requires an event participation record and a valid guest response channel; check-in requires an admission subject/credential or an explicitly supported manual lookup path. Neither should be a prerequisite for a venue booking.

### 4. Responsibility is explicit and can be delegated

For each enabled module or operational task, record who is accountable and who performs, approves or is informed. Parties may be the venue provider, organizer, an authorized collaborator or an external party. A task may also be marked not applicable or managed outside Eventor.

Avoid a vague global assumption that "the organization" is responsible for every event task. Responsibility is scoped to a booking/event and task/module, and can be overridden when the arrangement changes.

### 5. Keep data collection proportional to the venue service

For venue-provider-only use, collect only what is reasonably needed to process the inquiry, make the agreement, reserve the venue/resources and deliver the contracted venue services. Guest-level information, invitations, RSVP answers, seating assignments and organizer-side coordination records are not required by default.

If an organizer elects to use Eventor's event modules, the system may collect the additional data needed for those features under the appropriate access, privacy, retention and audit controls.

### 6. Collaboration is explicit

A booking customer or event organizer does not automatically become a tenant, organization member or user of the venue provider's Eventor installation. Cross-organization collaboration requires an explicit invitation or scoped access grant for the relevant booking/event and data projection. No broad tenant access is implied.

### 7. Preserve each party's own venue/facility duties

This operating model does not transfer, waive or determine statutory, regulatory or contractual responsibilities. The venue provider still manages its own venue, resource availability, facility constraints, house rules and contracted venue-side services. The organizer manages the event responsibilities assigned to it by the applicable arrangement. Eventor records operational ownership; it does not make legal determinations or certify compliance.

## Consequences

- A lightweight venue-provider installation can use Eventor as a booking/resource-management system without activating the guest/event-operations lifecycle.
- Organizer deployments can enable the full platform.
- Hybrid events can share work while keeping accountability and visibility explicit.
- Domain modeling must distinguish booking parties and the actual event organizer from the platform tenant.
- Event operations configuration needs organization defaults, event-level overrides, module dependencies and task-level responsibility assignments.
- Public and staff data projections must follow the minimum-necessary principle.
- The v0.2 schema and API are historical drafts and must not be extended ad hoc; a successor design revision must specify the operating-scope model before implementation.

# ADR 0005: Invitations, RSVP responses and attendance are separate lifecycles

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-10
- **Related:** [Issue #6](https://github.com/TeraflopsBH/eventor/issues/6), [ADR 0004](0004-optional-event-operations-scope.md)
- **Design detail:** [RSVP and Invitation Design v0.3](../implementation-design/v0.3/RSVP_AND_INVITATION_DESIGN_v0.3.md)

## Context

The v0.2 schema stores one `rsvp_status` on `event_guests` and uses general guest credentials for portal/admission access. This is insufficient for the agreed workflows: guests can respond through personalized links, staff can record responses received by phone/in person/email/writing/representatives, and actual attendance is a separate physical event.

Eventor also serves venue providers that may not organize the event or need any guest-level information. Guest operations must therefore be enabled only within the appropriate event scope and responsibility assignment.

## Decision

1. Invitation issuance/delivery, invitation-link validity, RSVP response, event participation/eligibility and physical attendance are distinct state dimensions.
2. RSVP responses are append-only history. The current response is a projection, not the only retained record.
3. Guest self-service RSVP uses a high-entropy, opaque, revocable invitation capability scoped to one event guest. It is not an admission QR and does not require a guest account by default.
4. Link resolution is non-destructive. GET requests, preview bots and email security scanners cannot submit a response or consume the invitation.
5. Staff may record outside-channel responses without a guest link/email. Capture records source, received time, system recording time, authenticated operator and optional restricted note. Corrections append history.
6. Guest response changes are governed by a versioned event RSVP policy, deadline and permissions; late staff overrides require a reason and audit.
7. RSVP/guest capabilities are optional modules. A venue-only booking requires no operational event or guest records. Guest data belongs to the assigned event-operating organization and is not visible to a venue provider merely because it supplied the space.
8. Public responses use allow-listed personal projections; no public guest directory or cross-guest access exists.

## Consequences

- The v0.2 `event_guests.rsvp_status` field must be separated from invitation and waitlist/eligibility state in a successor schema.
- A dedicated invitation record, link-credential lifecycle and response-history model are required.
- Notification delivery records need a reliable relationship to invitations.
- Public and staff API contracts require separate commands/projections and scoped authorization.
- RSVP implementation must not be coupled to check-in, seating or venue booking.
- The current v0.2 schema and OpenAPI files remain unchanged historical drafts; changes belong in a reviewed successor revision.

# ADR 0006: Keep venue and event data separately owned with explicit collaboration

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-10
- **Related:** ADR 0004, [Issue #12](https://github.com/TeraflopsBH/eventor/issues/12)
- **Design proposal:** [Cross-Organization Collaboration v0.3](../implementation-design/v0.3/CROSS_ORGANIZATION_COLLABORATION_DESIGN_v0.3.md)

## Context

ADR 0004 makes venue-provider and event-organizer responsibilities distinct. They may be different organizations. The v0.2 schema does not fully support this case because many composite foreign keys assume the booking, venue and operational event all share one organization_id. In particular, booking-to-event links, event-session-to-space links and guest-allocation-to-resource links are same-organization relationships.

A common real-world case is GHB owning a venue and booking record while an independent conference organizer owns the event, guest list, invitations, RSVP, seating decisions and attendance.

## Proposed decision

1. Keep venue master data, venue-space revisions, booking aggregates and venue-service fulfilment under the venue provider organization.
2. Keep event, guest registry, invitations, RSVP, seating decisions, attendance and organizer-side event operations under the organization assigned to operate the event/module.
3. External customers do not automatically become Eventor tenants or users. A booking-only workflow requires no operational-event data.
4. When both parties use the same Eventor deployment, create explicit collaboration grants and booking-event association records with distinct owner organization IDs.
5. Share approved venue geometry and resource inventory through immutable, purpose-limited event-owned snapshots that preserve source provider/revision/hash/grant provenance. Do not grant direct write access to provider master venue data.
6. Assign task/module accountability and performing parties explicitly. A task grant exposes only the minimum data needed to perform it.
7. No broad tenant membership or guest-data visibility is implied by booking, venue ownership or a collaboration link.

## Consequences

- The v0.2 same-organization foreign-key assumptions must be revised in a successor schema.
- A scoped collaboration grant and grant lifecycle are required.
- Booking-event linking must support separate owner organizations.
- Event sessions and allocations must reference event-owned shared venue snapshots/resources.
- RLS and authorization must remain tenant-isolated; collaboration uses explicit scoped projections.
- Historical venue snapshots and operational records remain auditable after grant expiry/revocation; new access is blocked.
- The product owner accepted this model on 2026-11-10. Schema/API implementation remains subject to review and tests, but the ownership and collaboration approach is the accepted architecture.


## Implementation integrity correction — migration 198

The existing authorized revocation command accepts proposed as well as active grants. A proposal withdrawn before acceptance must retain null acceptance actor/time. Migration 198 reconciles the original constraint with that command: active/expired grants still require genuine acceptance, revoked grants preserve whichever acceptance history actually occurred, and actor/time plus revocation/time pairing remain mandatory. This fixes an unreachable existing command path without inventing acceptance or changing collaboration permissions.

# ADR 0007: Make internationalization a cross-cutting platform capability

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-12
- **Related:** ADR 0001, ADR 0004, [Project state](../PROJECT_STATE.md)

## Context

Eventor is a self-hosted, multi-organization product. The reference deployment is in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the platform is intended for organizations and customers who may use different languages. The staff workspace is a Vue 3 application with a shared i18n runtime. Organization records have a persisted default locale as well as a default timezone; staff users have an optional global locale preference. Timezone is not a substitute for locale.

Adding translations after the staff and customer interfaces expand would require invasive changes and risk mixing translated labels with stable business values. Customer communications also need to be understandable in the recipient's language without changing the immutable commercial terms accepted by the customer.

## Decision

### 1. Locale identifiers and initial languages

1. Use canonical BCP 47 language tags, not translated names or arbitrary short codes, as locale identifiers.
2. Initial reference locales are `bs-BA` (Bosnian as used in Bosnia and Herzegovina) and `en` (English).
3. Keep locale identifiers separate from stable domain codes, database enum values, permission codes, API field names and workflow states. Translated display labels must never be used as identifiers.
4. Store translation catalogs as version-controlled application resources. Do not store application UI labels in tenant-editable database rows.

### 2. Staff locale resolution

Resolve the staff interface locale in this order:

1. Explicit, valid user preference.
2. Selected organization's configured default locale.
3. Deployment-wide fallback locale (`en`).

The user's preference is a presentation preference and applies across organizations. An organization default is a tenant configuration fallback, not a forced language. A user's preference must not alter another user's display or the language of a message already issued.

Locale values received from browsers, headers, query parameters or API clients must be validated against the deployment's supported-locale catalogue. Unsupported values fall back; they must not cause arbitrary locale loading or filesystem access.

### 3. Customer-facing locale resolution

Resolve a customer-facing page or communication using:

1. An explicit, validated language choice associated with that customer interaction or communication request.
2. A customer language preference, when one has been collected and is available for that purpose.
3. The owning organization's configured default locale.
4. The deployment fallback locale (`en`).

A public page may accept a locale hint, but the hint is presentation input only and cannot grant access or change the underlying booking/offer. Public booking inquiry submissions may include an explicit `customerLocale`; it is validated against the deployment's supported locales and stored on the inquiry. If omitted, the inquiry inherits the owning organization's `default_locale`. The resolved inquiry locale is carried into the public offer projection and queued offer-email job. Do not infer language from a person's name, nationality, location or other personal attributes.

### 4. Translation resources and authored content

1. UI translation keys are stable, namespaced identifiers (for example, `booking.offer.accept`); translated strings are resources, not keys.
2. Use a maintained Vue-compatible i18n library for the staff client rather than a home-grown interpolation/pluralization engine. Select the package and version in the implementation PR based on the existing Vue 3 toolchain.
3. Use standards-based locale formatting and plural rules (ECMA-402 `Intl` in JavaScript runtimes). Do not concatenate translated fragments to construct sentences.
4. Vendor-authored content that must be presented in multiple languages (for example, public descriptions, service descriptions, policy text and email templates) is distinct from application UI translation. Model translations as language-tagged content associated with a stable source record and preserve publication/revision semantics. Do not overwrite one language with another. For booking forms, optional `contentTranslations` live inside the immutable `booking_form_revisions.field_schema` snapshot, keyed by supported BCP 47 locale. Each locale carries the translated form name and field label, description, help text, placeholder and option labels; stable field codes and option values remain unchanged. The base revision locale remains the source-language fallback.
5. A missing authored-content translation must be visible to staff and follow a documented fallback policy; do not silently generate machine translations. Public booking forms fall back per content item to the immutable revision's base locale and tell the customer when any content remains in that language.
6. Email templates and other customer communication templates must be language-specific or resolve through a shared translation catalogue. The rendered communication and its locale must be retained with the delivery/audit record when needed to reproduce what was sent.

### 5. Dates, times, numbers and money

1. Locale controls presentation, not domain meaning.
2. Timezone remains an explicit domain value. Use the booking/event timezone for event and booking times; use the organization's timezone only where the domain explicitly calls for it. Never derive timezone from locale.
3. Store timestamps as instants and preserve the relevant IANA timezone separately where local scheduling meaning matters.
4. Store monetary values and ISO 4217 currency codes independently of locale. Locale formatting must not change the amount, currency, tax calculation or rounding.
5. Use locale-aware number, date, time, currency and plural formatting in both browser and server-rendered/customer-communication paths. Ensure server and browser resolve the same explicit locale and timezone to avoid inconsistent output.

### 6. Fallback and quality rules

1. Missing UI keys fall back to the deployment fallback locale and are reported by development/test tooling.
2. Missing customer-authored translation falls back only according to the content type's explicit policy; the interface should identify the language actually being shown where ambiguity matters.
3. Do not fall back to a different locale silently for legal, commercial or policy text where the recipient could reasonably believe the text is authoritative in the requested language. Such content must be explicitly marked unavailable or the communication must use an approved available language.
4. Translation catalogs must be UTF-8 and support full Unicode, including Bosnian Latin diacritics.
5. Tests must cover locale precedence, unsupported locale fallback, pluralization, formatting, missing keys and preservation of stable API/domain codes.

## Consequences

- Organization `default_locale`, inquiry `customer_locale` and optional global user `locale_preference` are persisted for the initial `bs-BA` and `en` locales. Organization default changes require `organization.manage`; user preference changes are scoped to the authenticated global user identity.
- The current staff workspace should be migrated incrementally from inline English strings to namespaced translation keys, beginning with shared navigation, authentication and common status/action labels.
- Customer-facing offer, booking inquiry, invitation/RSVP and cancellation communications must resolve and record an explicit locale before broader rollout.
- Vendor-authored translatable content needs a versioned translation model so historical offers, policies and sent messages remain reproducible.
- The reference deployment can begin with Bosnian and English without constraining future deployments to those languages.
- Locale and timezone remain separate configuration concerns; the existing `Europe/Sarajevo` timezone default is not a locale default.
- The implementation is delivered incrementally through stacked migration, API, frontend and regression-test pull requests. User preference is global; organization default remains tenant-scoped and is never a forced language.

## Implementation sequence

1. Add supported-locale catalogues and staff-client i18n runtime, migrate shared shell/authentication strings, and test fallback/plural/formatting behavior.
2. Persist organization defaults and global staff-user preferences, expose them through permission-appropriate API projections and settings commands, and test cross-tenant behavior. Implemented in the stacked locale-settings slice after PR #62.
3. Resolve and persist the locale on public booking inquiries, expose it only through the capability-protected customer offer projection, and use it for the queued offer email. Implemented in PR #62. The public booking form now initializes its interface from the organization default, permits an explicit Bosnian/English choice, and submits that choice with the inquiry; the immutable form revision's authored locale remains separate and is disclosed when it differs from the selected interface locale. Implemented in the stacked public-form locale slice. Extend the same contract to other customer communications and retain rendered template/content revisions with delivery evidence.
4. Add versioned translations for vendor-authored public descriptions, policy text and reusable templates as those administration workflows are implemented. Public booking form schema v1 now supports immutable `contentTranslations` for the form name and field/option text; API validation rejects unsupported locales, unknown field codes and unknown option values, while the public form renders the selected locale with explicit base-locale fallback. Migration 000068 adds tenant-scoped, permission-checked database commands for form listing, creation, draft revision creation/editing and immutable publication. The authenticated staff API now exposes these commands with idempotent mutations and reuses the same schema-v1 validator for draft content and translations. The editor, translation completeness review and locale previews remain follow-up slices.
5. Extend the same locale contract to guest portal, invitations/RSVP, cancellation notices, check-in and operational interfaces.

Each step must remain independently reviewable. Do not translate the entire interface in one change or combine locale behavior with unrelated commercial workflow changes.

# ADR 0008: Keep staff frontend modular and feature-oriented

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-12
- **Related:** ADR 0001, ADR 0007

## Context

The staff application currently places most application state, API orchestration, formatting helpers and multiple workflows in a single `App.vue`. This makes unrelated features difficult to review independently and creates friction for translation, testing and future contributors. Adding i18n to that file would reinforce the existing concentration of responsibilities.

## Decision

1. Keep `App.vue` as a thin application composition/root component. It may own top-level route selection and compose feature views, but must not become the home for every workflow.
2. Organize substantial product areas as feature modules (for example, booking inquiries, offers, approvals, pricing, cancellation policies, tax configuration and email delivery).
3. Place reusable presentational controls and layout primitives in a shared component area; keep feature-specific components with their owning feature.
4. Move reusable Vue state and behavior into focused composables. Keep API transport and endpoint contracts in API/client modules, not inside presentational components.
5. Keep domain calculations and formatting independent of component templates. Locale-aware formatting belongs in shared i18n/formatting utilities and must receive explicit locale/timezone context.
6. Keep translation catalogues grouped by language and stable feature namespaces. Do not scatter translated strings across components or use translated labels as domain values.
7. Avoid premature fragmentation: split by responsibility and stable feature boundary, not by creating a component for every wrapper or line of markup.
8. New UI work must follow this structure. Existing monolithic sections should be extracted incrementally as they are next modified; do not perform a risky all-at-once rewrite.

## Consequences

- New feature work can be reviewed and tested in smaller units.
- `App.vue` remains temporarily large until existing workflows are extracted; this ADR does not claim that the legacy monolith has already been decomposed.
- The i18n foundation is a first modular boundary: locale catalogues, runtime setup and formatting utilities live outside the root component.
- Subsequent extraction should prioritize feature views and API/state composables, preserving behavior and authorization checks.


## Incremental extraction record

The first extraction moves booking-inquiry presentation logic into `src/features/booking-inquiries/presentation.ts`: answer-value formatting, assignee display-name resolution, inquiry date display and booking-money display. The module depends only on the API's inquiry data types and explicit inputs; it does not own network calls or authorization decisions. Existing behavior is preserved while the root component delegates to the feature module. Next extraction should move inquiry state and API orchestration into a focused composable, then isolate the inquiry view, rather than attempting a wholesale rewrite.


The next extraction after presentation helpers moves booking-inquiry state and command orchestration into `src/features/booking-inquiries/useBookingInquiries.ts`. The composable receives shared application dependencies explicitly and exposes state/actions to the root composition layer. The existing inquiry template remains in `App.vue` at this stage; a dedicated feature view is a later step. Server-side authorization remains authoritative, with capability checks retained in the client for presentation and interaction gating.


The next extraction moves booking-inquiry state and command orchestration into `src/features/booking-inquiries/useBookingInquiries.ts`. The composable receives shared application dependencies explicitly and exposes state/actions to the root composition layer. The existing inquiry template remains in `App.vue`; a dedicated feature view is a later step. Server-side authorization remains authoritative, with capability checks retained in the client for presentation and interaction gating.


The next extraction isolates the booking-inquiry workspace presentation in `src/features/booking-inquiries/BookingInquiryView.vue`. The view receives the feature composable's state and actions through an explicit workspace prop and emits the action that opens the booking draft. The inquiry inbox/detail/review/annotation/history UI is feature-owned. Booking-draft editing and commercial offer/approval/confirmation markup remain in the root composition layer and are supplied through named slots, avoiding an accidental expansion of this view extraction into the separate commercial workflow. The root retains shared session lifecycle, booking-draft state and offer orchestration.


Booking-draft workflow state and commands form a separate feature module at `src/features/booking-drafts/useBookingDraft.ts`. It owns the selected draft and revision editor state, capability-derived editability, loading/refresh, revision creation and reset. The root composition layer supplies shared dependencies and coordinates the selected inquiry's draft reference. Offer preparation, delivery, approvals and confirmation remain a distinct commercial-offer workflow and should be extracted separately rather than coupled into the booking-draft composable.

The commercial offer lifecycle is extracted into `src/features/booking-offers/useBookingOffers.ts`. This cohesive feature owns offer preparation and successor revisions, issuance, customer capability handling, SMTP delivery queue/reconciliation/retry, approval decisions and explicit booking confirmation. It receives the shared API/session/message state and booking-draft/inquiry refresh dependencies from the root composition layer. Price-list, cancellation-policy and tax-profile administration remain separate configuration workflows; this extraction does not change their API behavior or the server's authority over permissions and final availability.

Commercial configuration is split by domain rather than collected in one generic composable: price lists, tax profiles, approval policies and cancellation policies each have a dedicated feature composable under `src/features/`. The price-list feature consumes the tax feature's published-revision projection through an explicit dependency to filter compatible currency/tax-basis revisions. The root component remains the composition boundary for shared API/session/busy/message state and currently hosts the corresponding workspace markup; feature view components can be extracted separately without coupling domain state or API orchestration.


The four commercial-configuration workspace templates are extracted into feature-owned views under their corresponding feature directories. Each view receives the matching composable return contract through a typed `workspace` prop and the shared busy reference; it owns presentation only and does not instantiate an API client or duplicate workflow state. `App.vue` composes the views by active workspace and retains only the cross-feature tax-profile projection needed by price-list configuration. This keeps the four domains independently reviewable while preserving the existing UI and command boundaries.


Campaign review and delivery reporting follow the same boundary: `features/campaigns/useCampaigns.ts` owns campaign and delivery state/commands, while `CampaignWorkspaceView.vue` renders the workspace from an explicit typed contract. Shared session messages, busy state and SMTP readiness remain application-level dependencies passed into the feature. The root no longer owns campaign lookup, delivery reconciliation/retry, or campaign lifecycle command implementations.


The organization email-delivery workspace is extracted into `src/features/email-delivery/useEmailDelivery.ts` and `EmailDeliveryView.vue`. The composable owns SMTP configuration state, write-only credentials, explicit credential clearing, revision save/test behavior and the optional Resend callback lifecycle. The view owns the existing readiness/configuration UI and receives a typed workspace contract. `App.vue` retains session-level composition and shares the email configuration readiness with campaign operations. This does not make Resend a required sending provider: organization-owned SMTP remains the generic delivery interface, while Resend callbacks are conditionally available for the Resend SMTP host.


The application shell and staff session lifecycle are extracted into `src/features/application-shell/`: `useStaffSession.ts` owns principal/session restoration, sign-in/out, selected-organization display and centralized API error handling, while `StaffApplicationShell.vue` owns the shared login/authenticated shell, locale selector, navigation, notices and footer. Session error/sign-out cleanup is delegated through an explicit reset callback to keep feature lifecycle ownership in the feature modules. The public customer offer capability-link flow is separately rendered in `src/features/public-booking-offers/PublicBookingOfferPage.vue`; it is not nested in the staff workspace shell. `App.vue` is the composition boundary for public-route selection and staff feature composition.


The booking-draft editor and commercial offer workspace presentation are extracted into `src/features/booking-drafts/CommercialBookingWorkspaceView.vue`. The view provides separate `draft-editor` and `offer-workspace` modes to fit the existing named slots in `BookingInquiryView.vue`, and consumes a typed intersection of the draft and offer composable contracts. It owns no API client or workflow state. `App.vue` now only composes the draft and offer composables and passes their combined workspace to the view; immutable draft revisions, offer issuance/delivery, approval decisions and explicit booking confirmation remain in their existing feature composables.


The inquiry presentation helpers now require explicit locale and timezone inputs. A feature-owned `useInquiryPresentation.ts` composable bridges Vue I18n's active locale and the browser-resolved local timezone into the pure date/currency formatting functions, and resolves the empty-date label from the common catalogue. All booking inquiry and commercial configuration views that display these values use the shared presentation composable. Locale changes therefore affect presentation reactively; stored timestamps, ISO currency codes, exact monetary values and domain calculations remain unchanged.


The booking inquiry and commercial booking workspace views consume feature-scoped `bookingInquiry` and `commercialBooking` namespaces from both locale catalogues. Domain status values remain the untranslated `value` of controls and API payloads; only their displayed labels are localized. Commercial identifiers, codes, currency values, tax-allocation method tokens, immutable snapshots and user-entered text are not translated. This keeps language selection strictly at the presentation boundary.


The public booking-offer capability page uses the `publicOffer` feature namespace and an explicit customer language choice rather than inferring language from customer identity or location. Locale-aware date/number formatting follows that choice; customer-entered and organization-authored commercial terms remain untouched.


Booking workflow composables receive a typed translation function from `App.vue` rather than owning or importing a locale runtime. Client-owned validation, confirmation prompts, success/error notices and JSON parsing feedback use the feature catalogues. This keeps locale selection at the application boundary and makes workflow copy react to locale changes without changing domain values, API behavior or server-originated error messages.

Commercial-configuration workflow composables follow the same localization boundary as inquiry and offer workflows: `App.vue` supplies the active translator, while each feature composable owns its domain validation and command orchestration. Client-owned confirmations, validation feedback and success notices resolve through the `commercialConfiguration` catalogue in English and Bosnian. The composables remain independent of Vue I18n runtime imports; domain values and server-originated API errors are not rewritten. Static configuration-view copy is localized in the feature views through dedicated Vue I18n namespaces.

The four commercial-configuration views resolve their static copy and display-only enum/status labels through feature-scoped Vue I18n namespaces (`priceView`, `taxView`, `approvalView`, `cancelView`) in English and Bosnian. Views translate labels, help copy and displayed enum labels while retaining the original API/domain values in form models, selectors and payloads. Configuration composables remain translator-injected and independent of Vue I18n; locale selection remains at the application/view boundary.

Campaign and email-delivery workspaces follow the same localization boundary: static view copy is resolved through feature-scoped Vue I18n namespaces (`campaignWorkspace`, `emailDelivery`), while client-owned workflow feedback is translated by the composables through a typed translator injected by `App.vue`. Display-only status labels are localized without changing domain values. The application locale is also used when formatting campaign timestamps. External protocol identifiers and provider-specific event names remain literal.

The application shell uses the active locale for visible and accessibility labels. `useStaffSession` remains Vue-I18n-independent and receives the typed translator from `App.vue` for client-owned session messages; server-originated API error details are preserved rather than rewritten by the client.

Stable API problem codes are localized at the staff presentation boundary through `src/i18n/api-errors.ts`. The helper accepts the API error and an injected translator, maps known codes to the `apiErrors` catalogue, and preserves the server title/code for unknown future codes. `useStaffSession` remains the shared error-presentation boundary for staff feature composables; the public booking-offer page reuses the same formatter with its explicit customer locale. The API contract and server-originated error payloads remain unchanged.


A follow-up presentation audit of the commercial booking workspace keeps all staff-authored labels, action captions and explanatory placeholders in the `commercialBooking` locale catalogue. Existing feature keys are reused where semantics match; new keys cover the remaining draft/offer placeholders and offer reference labels. Technical JSON/ISO/currency examples and protocol identifiers remain literal, and locale changes do not alter submitted values or workflow behavior.


The staff UI localization audit also covers accessible names and browser-native constraint validation. Interactive controls retain explicit localized labels or meaningful visible text; brand names remain proper names. HTML constraint-validation messages remain browser-owned and are not duplicated as application translations. Residual application-owned fallback copy must use the feature catalogue, including the inquiry list's missing-requested-date label.

# ADR 0009: Reversible Guest Registry merge

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-17
- **Related:** [Issue #104](https://github.com/TeraflopsBH/eventor/issues/104), Technical Blueprint v1.2 §33.4

## Decision

Registry managers with `guest.registry.merge` can review two active profiles within one organization. The operator selects the destination, compares both profiles and confirms that the source is a duplicate. Commit requires a review recorded for the current actor, checks the reviewed revisions and uses the destination names as the resolved fields.

The initial implementation required an eligible source to have zero event participations, contact points, identifiers and incoming merge references. Later accepted extensions preserve closed-event references and permit the reviewed contact transfer described below. The command preserves the source row, marks it merged and records the identity references and resolution. Event snapshots stay associated with their existing participation records. The merge history records staff attribution, the reason and the timestamps.

A reviewer can restore the source from merge history. Restoration reactivates the source with its own name values and records the correction. A stale or externally altered source requires investigation before it can be restored through this workflow.

Merge planning for linked profiles requires explicit resolution of event, contact and identifier conflicts, with a correction workflow for each affected record.

## Reviewed non-conflicting contact transfer — 2026-11-24

A reviewer with both Registry merge and contact-management authority can explicitly move every supported email/phone contact from the duplicate source to the destination. The review displays both contact sets and requires a separate transfer confirmation. Contact IDs, encrypted values, normalized fingerprints, consent, primary flags and verification evidence are preserved. Encryption remains bound to the same organization and contact kind, so ownership reassignment does not require decryption or re-encryption in SQL.

Competing primary contacts, duplicate values and unsupported legacy contact kinds require separate resolution and block this command. Unsupported identifiers, active relationships, open/overlapping event history and incoming merge references retain their existing guards. Reviewed source-reference transfer is defined in [ADR 0012](0012-reference-encryption-identity.md). No contact is discarded, deduplicated or given more permissive consent by a merge.

Both parent profiles are locked in stable order. Review evidence binds the exact source and destination contact IDs/revisions as well as profile and historical-event revisions. The existing name/history transition is reused through private helpers; runtime callers cannot bypass the transfer boundary. An append-only, tenant-scoped transfer journal records only merge/contact references and expected transferred revisions. API idempotent retries recheck contact-management authority.

Restoration requires the same additional authority and atomically returns the transferred contacts, with their original IDs and protected facts, to the reactivated source. Contact revisions advance on transfer and restoration. If any transferred contact has subsequently changed, restoration refuses to overwrite or reassign that changed record; the merge, current contact facts and journal remain intact. A separate reviewed correction is required for that case. Do not reset revisions or alter the journal to force restoration. This extension does not complete the broader linked-record conflict-resolution scope of #104.


## Competing primary contacts — review assistance, 2026-11-24

When the server reports a contact conflict, the staff comparison can load both contact sets through the existing separately authorized contact APIs. For competing primary contacts of one kind, staff can explicitly clear one primary flag through the ordinary revision-checked, audited contact-preference command. This immediately edits that contact; it preserves consent, value and verification, and requests a fresh merge review. A cancelled confirmation leaves the contact unchanged. A stale edit requires reloading the comparison and cannot overwrite newer contact preferences.

This is an independent contact edit: restoring a later merge preserves the reviewed primary flags that existed at transfer. Merge remains a separate confirmed command with a fresh transfer acknowledgement. The server still rejects duplicate values and every other unsupported conflict. No automatic deduplication, deletion or consent combination is introduced.

# ADR 0010 — Organization membership access

- Status is accepted.
- Date is 2026-11-23.
- Related work is [Issue #104](https://github.com/TeraflopsBH/eventor/issues/104).

## Decision

Organization managers can suspend and restore organization memberships through an audited, revision-checked command. The command supports active and suspended memberships. Existing invitation and revocation states retain their own workflows.

Suspension revokes all current sessions for the selected membership in that organization. Restoring access preserves the member's role grants and requires a fresh login and an active global user. Other memberships for the same user retain their sessions.

Administrative writes use the existing organization access lock. Suspending a member requires another active user with an active organization-wide organization.manage grant. This preserves an administrator who can restore access. The UI confirms session revocation before suspension.

## Verification

Synthetic tests cover tenant and actor boundaries, revisions, session revocation, restoration, retained role grants and preservation of an active administrator. Browser acceptance exercises the manager's confirmation and the resulting member state.

# ADR 0011 — Database UUID compatibility

- Status is accepted.
- Date is 2026-11-23.

## Decision

UUID identifiers use canonical hexadecimal text with the 8-4-4-4-12 grouping accepted by the existing PostgreSQL schema. API, client input and cryptographic tenant-context validation accept persisted identifiers whose version or variant bits differ from newly generated version-4 UUIDs.

Authentication continues to derive the principal from an active database session, user, membership and organization. Permission checks continue to bind every operation to that principal. Contact and delivery encryption continue to authenticate the complete normalized organization identifier.

## Evidence

A synthetic provider account could log in successfully but its next authenticated request returned 401 because its existing database UUIDs used zero version and variant bits. Tests cover authenticated route access for those identifiers, malformed-path rejection, organization scope and cross-tenant encryption failure.
