# PostgreSQL integrity and concurrency test matrix — v0.3

This matrix tracks executable PostgreSQL integration coverage and remaining gaps for the v0.3 successor schema. A checked item has a corresponding assertion in the current CI suite; unchecked items remain future test work. API authorization cases require route-level tests and are not proven by database constraints alone.

## Tenant relationships
- [x] Same-organization person merge target accepted.
- [x] Cross-organization person merge target rejected.
- [x] Same-organization credential replacement is accepted; the delivery-configuration smoke test replaces the credential envelope with distinct bytes and verifies the new envelope is used by the SMTP test command.
- [x] Cross-organization credential replacement is rejected with SQLSTATE 42501 when an active membership from another tenant invokes the organization-scoped command.
- [x] User actor with active membership in owning organization accepted.
- [ ] User with no membership in owning organization rejected.
- [ ] Member without operation permission rejected by API authorization.
- [x] Cross-organization delegated task projection/status command succeeds only with an active grant naming the exact task ID and a local `task.perform` role permission; its audit row records the performer in the event owner’s tenant.
- [ ] Expired grant blocks new access without erasing historical records.
- [x] Revoked grant blocks new booking links, event snapshots, session bindings and snapshot child additions without deleting historical records.

## Global identity and authentication boundary
- [x] General runtime cannot SELECT, INSERT or update global user identity/password-hash rows directly.
- [x] Authentication role can resolve users and their organization memberships but cannot read venue/booking/event business data or mutate memberships.
- [x] Tenant-filtered member-profile view exposes only the active organization’s membership/profile projection.
- [x] Database-backed staff sessions store only SHA-256 hashes of opaque session/CSRF tokens, bind to one user/organization/membership tuple, expire and revoke server-side, and are hidden from runtime/worker roles.
- [x] Authentication-role CI checks cover session/rate-limit table privileges; API tests cover Argon2id login, origin allow-list, CSRF double-submit, active membership lookup and revocation.

## Cross-organization grant and RLS lifecycle
- [x] Grantor and grantee can see their own shared grant row; unrelated tenant cannot.
- [x] Only an active member of the grantor organization can propose a grant.
- [x] Proposal, first grant revision and audit event are written atomically.
- [x] Only an active member of the grantee organization can accept a grant.
- [x] Repeated acceptance by the same actor is idempotent and does not duplicate the audit record.
- [x] Booking-event link ending/revocation and venue snapshot share revocation/expiry require an active local membership plus reason code and write one lifecycle audit record.
- [x] Grantee cannot invoke the grantor-side revocation command.
- [x] Grantor can revoke; grantee retains historical visibility while the grant is marked revoked.
- [x] Revoked grant blocks new venue snapshot copies, booking-event links, session bindings and new snapshot child rows.
- [x] Venue snapshot share is constrained to grant scope, validity window and exact published source revision/content hash.
- [x] Provider-approved layer/resource IDs must belong to the exact source revision/venue; duplicates and foreign IDs are rejected.
- [x] Copied snapshot layers must match approved source layers; each copied object must map to the exact copied layer for its source object's layer; copied resources must match approved pool/unit IDs.
- [x] Recipient RLS exposes only approved source rows while the share and grant are active.
- [x] A read-only `venue.snapshot.read` grant can SELECT its approved source revision but cannot create/use an event snapshot.
- [x] Revocation hides provider-owned source rows from the recipient but retains its already-copied event-owned snapshot.

## Venue hierarchy
- [x] Valid organization → venue → building → level → space accepted.
- [x] Space pointing to a building from a different venue is rejected by the composite organization/venue/building foreign key; `tests/database/migration_smoke.sql` attempts the cross-venue reference and requires a foreign-key violation.
- [x] Space pointing to a level from another building rejected.
- [x] Space with a level but no building rejected.
- [x] Cross-organization hierarchy reference rejected.

## Configuration integrity
- [x] Catalogue revision includes option and the option's own revision.
- [x] Option revision belonging to another stable option rejected.
- [x] Option from a different catalogue revision rejected.
- [ ] Retired option remains historically readable but cannot be newly selected where policy forbids it.
- [x] Published catalogue and option revisions reject UPDATE/DELETE.
- [x] Published catalogue membership rejects new child rows.
- [x] Published form revisions and form-to-catalogue bindings reject mutation.
- [x] Published venue-space revisions and spatial layer/object children reject mutation or late additions.
- [x] Concurrent revision publication and child insertion use independent connections; the insert waits on the parent lock and is rejected after publication commits.
- [ ] Published price-list, cancellation-policy, RSVP-policy, notification-template and event-capability revisions have dedicated mutation regression cases.
- [x] Cancellation effects reject an unpinned policy revision and preserve the explicit NULL/no-policy booking snapshot.

## Space reservations
- [x] Adjacent half-open intervals (10:00–11:00 and 11:00–12:00) both succeed.
- [x] Identical/overlapping intervals for the same room cannot both be active.
- [x] A released space hold cannot be revived; a new hold cannot be inserted with an already-expired deadline.
- [x] Runtime and worker roles cannot UPDATE/DELETE space-time block rows directly; lifecycle changes use controlled commands.
- [x] Accepted draft resource and space holds are converted atomically to confirmed booking reservations through a permission-gated command; retries do not duplicate occupancy or audit history.
- [x] Cancelled booking reservations are released only by caller-selected IDs (resource and/or space rows); mixed invalid IDs are rejected atomically, partial release leaves unselected rows intact, and retries emit no duplicate audit.
- [x] Editable booking drafts can release explicitly selected live resource/space holds during amendment or reallocation through a runtime-only, permission-gated command; exact IDs, actor/reason audit attribution, retry idempotency, mixed-invalid-ID atomic rejection, accepted-offer protection and resource/space locking are exercised by the commercial end-to-end fixture.
- [x] Overlap is rejected even when one claim originated as a temporary hold and the other as a booking reservation (the commercial end-to-end fixture attempts a new overlapping draft hold after confirming the booking and asserts SQLSTATE 23P01 plus no persisted hold).
- [x] Released/cancelled/expired interval no longer blocks a new reservation (CI releases a cancelled booking's selected space reservation, expires an overdue draft hold through `expire_space_holds`, retains a cancelled draft hold, then verifies the runtime role can create a new overlapping hold).
- [ ] Hold extension that creates a conflict is rejected atomically.
- [x] Booking with multiple spaces/times commits all or none (the commercial end-to-end fixture verifies incomplete two-space confirmation leaves the existing hold untouched, then confirms both space/time reservations together).
- [x] Concurrent overlapping space-hold transactions on separate runtime connections result in at most one active reservation; the second transaction waits for the first commit and then receives exclusion SQLSTATE 23P01.
- [ ] Reschedule conflict leaves the prior confirmed schedule unchanged.

- [ ] A space-time block has exactly one typed, tenant-safe origin reference.
- [ ] A hold-to-booking conversion retains continuous exclusion protection under concurrent confirmation/expiry.
- [x] Expiry worker and runtime reservation conversion serialize on the same hold row; an independent-login worker-first regression proves conversion waits for expiry commit and cannot convert the terminal hold.

## Equipment/personnel
- [x] Same discrete unit cannot be reserved for overlapping time.
- [x] Different discrete units in one pool can hold overlapping intervals within the booking-line quantity; `review_regressions.sql` reserves four distinct units for the same interval and rejects a fifth.
- [x] Pooled capacity is never exceeded under concurrent requests.
- [x] A booking resource line’s peak simultaneous quantity cannot be exceeded across separate pools.
- [x] Individually tracked unit reservations are included in the booking resource line quantity limit; a fifth overlapping unit is rejected when the requested quantity is four.
- [x] Pooled and individually tracked reservations share one aggregate pool-capacity invariant.
- [x] Pooled reservation idempotency compares the booking resource line as part of the payload.
- [x] Disjoint sub-interval reservations that both intersect a long requested interval are evaluated by peak simultaneous quantity, not incorrectly summed across the entire interval.
- [x] Adjacent half-open pool intervals do not count as simultaneous.
- [x] Expired pooled and individually tracked holds are expired by the worker; pool capacity is reclaimed and the same discrete unit can be reserved again.
- [ ] Resource line request/approval/delivery values remain separate from actual reservation records.

## Event cancellation, postponement and guest communications
- [x] Cancellation after invitations were delivered preserves invitation records, RSVP answers (accepted/tentative/declined/pending), completed-session state and attendance history.
- [x] Cancelling an event revokes outstanding invitation links, suppresses queued/failed invitation sends, preserves already delivered history, and rejects new invitation, link, delivery and RSVP activity.
- [x] Cancellation notification audience snapshots include all active invitees, including declined and unanswered invitees; queued campaign recipient sets and audience rules are immutable.
- [x] Postponement preserves original RSVP answers on the original schedule revision, retires old links/pending sends, and allows new invitation/RSVP activity only against the replacement schedule.
- [x] New postponement and reschedule requests both require a pinned replacement schedule revision; migration preflight stops rather than inventing schedule data for legacy postponed requests without one.
- [x] Postponement reconfirmation audience snapshot selects accepted/tentative invitees and excludes declined/unanswered invitees.
- [x] A provider booking-disruption notice alone does not cancel/postpone the organizer-owned event or create a guest-notification campaign; an explicit organizer decision is required.
- [x] Event decision kind must match its executed change request; notification campaign purpose and published template must match the decision.
- [x] Organizer event-change submission checks active membership, event-scoped initiation/postponement permission, current event revision and one unresolved request per event.
- [x] Approval/rejection and execution are separate permission-gated commands; execution records the decision, status history, session outcomes, audit event and transactional notification outbox atomically.
- [x] Cancellation, postponement and rescheduling commands enforce the event decision/status mapping; stale revisions, missing event scope and cross-tenant actors are rejected.
- [x] Runtime API route tests cover fail-closed staff authentication and CSRF/origin checks, private-reason encryption, Idempotency-Key replay/conflict and custom-audience input validation.
- [x] Worker-only tenant-scoped outbox processing prepares a fixed, reviewable campaign preview from accepted/tentative, active-invitee, previously-invited or custom audience rules; verified permitted contact snapshots remain encrypted and exclusions are retained.
- [x] Worker processing is idempotent, locks outbox rows with SKIP LOCKED, retries with bounded backoff and dead-letters after the configured attempt ceiling; worker tests prove no delivery attempts are created during preparation.
- [x] Organizer campaign review returns the fixed recipient snapshot, channel totals, exclusion totals and published template content without exposing encrypted contact values.
- [x] Campaign confirmation requires event-scoped send permission, a current matching event decision, a complete recipient-count snapshot and an active published template; confirmation is attributed in audit history.
- [x] Runtime cannot directly mutate campaign/recipient/exclusion/delivery tables; campaign confirmation does not queue delivery or create delivery attempts.
- [ ] Email/SMS delivery-provider adapter, callback handling and delivery retries.

## Append-only and issued business history
- [x] Runtime role lacks UPDATE/DELETE privileges on append-only history tables.
- [x] Table triggers also reject UPDATE/DELETE when executed by the table owner.
- [x] Booking draft revisions reject UPDATE/DELETE.
- [x] Invitation revisions reject UPDATE/DELETE under owner-level access; `event_cancellation_postponement_smoke.sql` uses a fixture revision and requires SQLSTATE 55000 for both operations.
- [x] Issued offer terms reject mutation; only one terminal offer decision transition is permitted.
- [x] Booking-event link grant provenance is written to audit history and substantive link fields cannot be rewritten.
- [x] Booking-event link and venue snapshot share lifecycle transitions are one-way and auditable.

## Optional modules and responsibility
- [ ] New event has no guest/invitation/RSVP/check-in/prerequisite/cockpit modules unless explicitly enabled by its event preset or configuration.
- [ ] Booking-only flow is possible with no event/guest records.
- [ ] Module-specific routes return a safe disabled/not-enabled error when capability is off.
- [ ] RSVP does not depend on check-in or seating.
- [ ] Check-in does not require accepted RSVP.
- [x] Delegated task projection/status operations expose only an allowlisted task view and require a task-specific cross-organization grant plus local role permission.
- [ ] Each assigned task has accountable/performed party and scoped visibility for event-owner management and every optional task projection.
- [ ] Venue provider cannot read organizer guest/RSVP data through booking or task links unless a narrowly scoped grant authorizes the exact projection.

## Execution requirements
Run against the supported PostgreSQL version with the non-owner application role. Concurrency tests must use multiple independent connections/processes. Record migration version, server version, test command and output in CI artifacts.

# PostgreSQL migration conventions

**Status:** accepted implementation baseline; target PostgreSQL major version: 18. Reconfirm the exact supported minor release when CI and deployment images are pinned.

These conventions apply to successor migrations. PostgreSQL 18 is the minimum target major for the first implementation baseline; use the latest supported PostgreSQL 18 minor release in CI and deployment, and do not target PostgreSQL 19 until it is a final supported release. The design uses the trusted `btree_gist` extension for GiST equality/range exclusion constraints; the extension package must be installed in the target environment and its availability tested before migrations. The imported v0.2 SQL remains a reference and must not be placed directly into production as-is. See [Database Review v0.2](DATABASE_REVIEW_v0.2.md).

## 1. Migration files and history

- Use ordered, immutable, human-readable migration names, for example `000001_create_organization_core.sql`.
- A migration is applied once and recorded in a migration ledger with version, filename, checksum, applied timestamp, execution duration and runner identity.
- Never silently edit a migration already applied to any shared environment. Correct it with a new forward migration.
- Keep schema changes and data migrations explicit. Large/backfill operations should be separately planned and observable.
- Do not use `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` as a substitute for migration ordering; unexpected schema drift must fail visibly.
- Migrations should be deterministic and safe to rerun only where the runner explicitly supports that behavior.

## 2. Transaction and search-path rules

A normal migration should own one transaction:

```sql
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL search_path TO eogp, public;

-- DDL / DML for this migration only.

COMMIT;
```

- Prefer schema-qualified object names for security-sensitive or ambiguous references.
- Use `SET LOCAL`, not session-persistent `SET search_path`, when a search path is required.
- Do not place nested `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` blocks inside a migration.
- Operations that PostgreSQL does not permit inside a transaction (for example some concurrent index operations) must be marked and executed by an explicit non-transactional migration mechanism.
- Acquire a migration lock so two deployers cannot apply migrations concurrently.

## 3. Database roles

Use separate roles with least privilege:
- **Schema owner:** owns schemas and objects; not used by application requests.
- **Migration role:** may create/alter objects and apply reviewed migrations.
- **Runtime role:** used by tenant-scoped API commands; does not own tables, is not superuser and does not have `BYPASSRLS`.
- **Authentication role:** dedicated `eventor_auth` credential for global user/password verification and organization-membership discovery. It does not have venue, booking, guest or event business-table access. The general runtime role has no direct access to `eogp.users`; tenant UI reads the RLS-filtered `eogp.organization_member_profiles` projection.

The API must not connect as the schema owner or migration role. Credentials are deployment secrets and are never stored in Git.

## 4. Tenant isolation and RLS

- Every tenant-owned row carries a non-null organization/tenant owner or has an explicit documented global/reference-data reason.
- Same-tenant foreign keys should include organization_id on both source and target columns.
- Cross-organization references must be explicit relationships with separate owner identifiers and an authorization grant; do not weaken same-tenant foreign keys to bare UUIDs.
- Enable and force RLS on tenant-owned tables where appropriate. Policies must default-deny and cover SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.
- Runtime tests must connect as the non-owner runtime role. Table owner/superuser tests do not prove RLS behavior.
- Set authenticated organization context transaction-locally after authorization and before queries; never trust an organization_id supplied only by a client.
- Ensure pooled connections cannot carry tenant context from one request into another.
- **The `app.organization_id` custom GUC is trusted application context, not a credential or cryptographic identity.** A database client that possesses the runtime credential and can execute arbitrary SQL can generally set that GUC itself. RLS therefore protects against omitted tenant predicates and accidental cross-tenant access; it does not make a compromised runtime credential safe from arbitrary SQL. Keep database credentials private to the API, prevent direct client/database access, use parameterized queries, constrain SECURITY DEFINER functions, and establish tenant context only inside authenticated/authorized transactions.

## 5. Integrity and concurrency

- Use database constraints for invariants where PostgreSQL can enforce them: FK, CHECK, UNIQUE, exclusion and appropriate partial indexes.
- Do not rely on an availability query or a B-tree overlap index to prevent double booking.
- Hold creation, confirmation, extension, release and expiry must serialize against the same resource reservation invariant.
- Use idempotency keys for commands that may be retried.
- Historical snapshots and response/audit histories are append-only at the application permission layer; use database protections where needed.
- Validate resource capacities and reservation quantities in the same transaction that commits the reservation.

## 6. Versioned configuration and reference data

- Stable option identity is separate from localized/presentation revision.
- Published revisions are immutable; publish a new revision instead of editing a live one.
- Retire used options; do not delete or repurpose their meaning.
- Inquiries, offers, bookings, invitations and RSVP responses pin the revisions/labels needed to reconstruct what was presented at the time.
- Seed only platform/system reference data in migrations. Organization-specific GHB catalogues, prices and venue geometry are separately reviewed, versioned configuration data.

## 7. Test requirements

Each schema migration must be tested against:
1. Empty supported PostgreSQL database.
2. The immediately preceding released schema version.
3. Valid synthetic fixtures.
4. Invalid foreign keys, cross-tenant references and check/unique/exclusion violations.
5. Concurrent conflicting operations where availability/capacity is involved.
6. The actual non-owner runtime role with RLS enabled.
7. Backup/restore and forward-recovery procedure appropriate to the change.

Record exact PostgreSQL major/minor version and command output in CI. No migration is considered validated merely because SQL text was accepted by a linter or because the application compiles.

# Eventor user roles and permission model — v0.1

**Status:** accepted baseline role and permission model; organization-specific assignments and thresholds remain subject to validation  
**Date:** 2026-11-10  
**Related:** [MVP Scope v0.1](MVP_SCOPE_v0.1.md), ADR 0004 and ADR 0006

Roles are permission bundles, not hardcoded job titles. An organization may create role presets, but the underlying permission catalogue and server-side checks remain authoritative. A user may hold different roles in different organizations or events. UI visibility alone never grants permission.

## 1. Principals and operating parties

Distinguish:
- Platform operator/administrator.
- Organization member.
- Venue provider.
- Booking customer/requester (may be an external contact with no account).
- Contracting party/payer (may differ from requester).
- Event organizer (may be an external party or a separate Eventor organization).
- External party/authority/vendor with no Eventor account.
- Service principal/background worker.

An external renter does not need a user account to submit an inquiry, accept a public offer through a scoped link if that workflow is enabled, or receive booking communications.

## 2. Proposed Release-1 roles

| Role | Typical permissions | Restrictions |
|---|---|---|
| Platform administrator | Platform configuration, tenant lifecycle, system health and platform-level support | Technical administration does not automatically grant guest-record, confidential-note or commercial-data access |
| Organization owner | Organization settings, memberships, operating profile, policy and high-level configuration | Cannot bypass audit or scope rules |
| Organization administrator | Staff/roles, venue configuration, published forms/catalogues and organization workflows | Sensitive operations may require additional approval |
| Booking manager | Inquiry inbox, clarification, booking drafts, quotes/offers, amendments and booking communication; review/coordinate cancellation requests and execute approved booking cancellations where granted | Cannot approve own restricted discount/exception or cancellation request unless policy explicitly permits |
| Booking approver / finance | Approve offers, discounts, exceptions and financial commitments within configured limits; approve/reject booking cancellation requests and their commercial consequences within assigned authority | No general access to guest/event operations unless separately assigned |
| Venue coordinator | Space calendar, setup/rehearsal/teardown, venue task assignments, readiness and issue handling; may initiate a venue-side cancellation for facility/service unavailability when explicitly granted | Only venue-side operational and booking data; cannot independently waive fees/refund terms unless separately authorised |
| Resource / technical coordinator | Equipment/personnel availability, service preparation, technical fulfilment and issue status | No unrelated commercial or personal data |
| Management read-only | Approved dashboards, aggregate reports and booking status | No write actions; field-filtered data |
| Auditor / compliance read-only | Permissioned audit and configuration history | Restricted, logged, read-only |
| External booking requester | Public inquiry, explicitly allowed offer/booking actions, submit a permitted cancellation request and view its limited status through a scoped secure action link | No tenant membership, approval authority, immediate cancellation right unless the pinned booking policy explicitly allows it, or access to internal notes/resources |

## 3. Later organizer/event roles

These roles are not required for a venue-only Release 1. They become available when the organization activates event operations:

| Role | Typical permissions |
|---|---|
| Event owner / event administrator | Event scope, capability activation, event policies and responsibility assignment; initiate/approve/execute event cancellation or postponement only with the corresponding scoped permissions |
| Guest coordinator | Guest Registry linkage, event participation, import, invitations and RSVP administration; prepare cancellation audience previews and communications when assigned |
| RSVP operator / reception | Staff-record response entry and permissioned response lookup |
| Seating coordinator | Venue snapshot use, allocation rules and manual/solver proposal review |
| Check-in operator | Admission validation and attendance recording using minimum necessary guest fields |
| Zone/floor coordinator | Only assigned operational map layers, zones and guest/task data |
| Event communications operator | Prepare/send event and cancellation notifications only for assigned events/audiences under an explicit task grant |
| Event operations manager | Cockpit, event alerts, task coordination and authorized interventions |
| External collaborator | Only the booking/event/task projection granted to its organization and role |

## 4. Permission design requirements

- Enforce permissions on every server operation and data query.
- Scope permissions by organization, venue, booking, event, space, station or assigned task where appropriate.
- Separate read/list, create, update, archive, approve, publish, export, grant/revoke and override permissions.
- Require explicit permissions for price/discount overrides, booking confirmation, guest export, RSVP deadline override, allocation approval/publication and attendance correction.
- Distinguish a user's organization membership from permission to perform a particular action.
- A collaboration grant authorizes only the named external organization/scope/projection; the user's membership and role in the grantee organization are still checked.
- External customer/organizer contact data stored in a booking does not grant access to the underlying tenant.
- Read/export of confidential or restricted information is audited as configured.
- Service jobs use a service principal identity and narrowly scoped permissions, not a shared human administrator account.

## 4.1 Cancellation authority is explicit

Role presets are defaults; the permission catalogue and booking/event policy determine actual authority.

| Scope | Initiate/request | Approve/reject | Execute/send |
|---|---|---|---|
| Booking customer | Authorised external contact may submit a cancellation request through a scoped action link | No authority by default | No direct effective cancellation unless the booking's pinned policy explicitly enables self-service |
| Venue booking | Venue coordinator or booking manager may initiate when granted | Booking approver/finance or configured authority | Designated booking manager/service after approval; emergency execution is a separate explicit permission and requires review |
| Organizer event | Event owner/admin may initiate cancellation or postponement | Event approver/owner under organizer policy | Designated event operator; guest campaign send permission is separately checked |
| Delegated guest communications | Named collaborator/operator may prepare the assigned campaign | Organizer's policy/approval rules still apply unless explicitly delegated | Only the assigned event/audience/action projection; no general guest-list access |

For the implemented staff inquiry workflow, the fine-grained permissions are `booking.inquiry.read`, `booking.inquiry.assign`, `booking.inquiry.manage`, `booking.inquiry.annotate`, `booking.inquiry.convert`, `booking.draft.read` and `booking.draft.manage`. Inquiry permissions authorize organization-scope inquiry actions before conversion and are checked against active organization-scope role grants while the inquiry remains unlinked. Draft permissions are also currently organization-scope because unconfirmed drafts do not have a `booking_records` row that can be targeted by a booking-scoped grant. A booking-scoped grant does not authorize access to an unlinked inquiry. Customer-visible notes and external requester actions require separate capability workflows.

Suggested fine-grained permissions (names to align with the successor catalogue) include `booking.cancellation.request`, `booking.cancellation.review`, `booking.cancellation.approve`, `booking.cancellation.execute`, `booking.cancellation.override`, `event.cancellation.initiate`, `event.cancellation.approve`, `event.cancellation.execute`, `event.postponement.manage` and `event.cancellation.notifications.send`.

Approval and execution may be separated to enforce dual control. Self-approval is disallowed for configured high-risk cancellation or commercial exceptions unless a documented organization policy explicitly permits it. Technical platform administration does not imply business cancellation authority.

## 5. Approval authority

The platform should support configurable approval chains and thresholds. Proposed defaults for a venue-provider deployment:
- Booking manager prepares the draft/offer.
- Authorized booking approver confirms pricing/discount exceptions.
- An authorized booking confirmer commits the reservation after availability is rechecked.
- A separate venue/resource coordinator owns setup and fulfilment task status.
- Self-approval is disallowed for configurable high-risk actions unless a documented organization policy permits it.

The actual GHB role names, limits, approval chains and separation-of-duties requirements must be confirmed by GHB. These are not assumed policies.

## 6. Test cases

- User in organization A cannot list/read/write organization B resources without an active scoped grant.
- Organization member with no booking permission cannot approve or confirm a booking.
- Booking manager cannot apply a discount beyond their threshold.
- Management read-only cannot mutate a booking.
- Platform technical administrator cannot read restricted guest notes merely by virtue of technical administration.
- Venue coordinator cannot access organizer guest lists or RSVP responses by default.
- External collaborator can access only the projection and task scope granted to its organization.
- Revoking a grant prevents new operations immediately; historical audit remains available to authorized owners.
- Service principal cannot invoke human-only approval actions unless a specific machine permission is granted and the workflow explicitly permits it.

## Approved OAC governance clarification — 2026-11-27

See [OAC v1.0](../implementation-design/v0.3/ORGANIZATION_ADMINISTRATION_CENTER_DESIGN_v1.0.md) and [UX v1.0](../implementation-design/v0.3/EVENTOR_USER_EXPERIENCE_AND_NAVIGATION_v1.0.md). Organization owner/administrator is tenant-scoped, not platform Owner/Superadmin. The initial tenant administrator is explicitly designated by PAC; subsequent tenant staff invitations, existing identity enrollment, memberships, role assignment, suspension/restoration and delegation use reviewed scoped commands. Membership is not authority. Preserve ADR 0010 last-active-administrator guard and independent memberships, ADR 0015 context/session boundaries and host-managed restrictions, ADR 0017/0020 protected host fallback, and PAC's reviewed successor ADR requirement before changing broad managed grants. No tenant owner can self-escalate to platform, inspect another tenant, globally reset another person's identity, or grant permissions beyond approved delegation ceilings. Role-based landing/navigation reflects effective permissions plus supported/activated capabilities, never a substitute for server checks. Routine onboarding should not require platform support; sensitive support uses actual actor and explicitly scoped PAC intervention. Preserve all original role and approval rules. Owner approved the three v1.0 scopes for documentation integration on 2026-11-27. The three reviewed source files are preserved verbatim, including their historical proposed-status text; this approval record governs their integration status, not approval of exact engineering decisions or immediate implementation. Existing accepted ADRs, historical Blueprint v1.2/v0.2 snapshots, issue obligations and current #104/#112 → #105–107 priorities remain unchanged. No runtime implementation or acceptance results are implied.

## Approved coordinated design permission clarification — 2026-11-27

[AES v1.0](../implementation-design/v0.3/ADAPTIVE_EXPERIENCE_AND_SETUP_DESIGN_v1.0.md), [EPW v1.0](../implementation-design/v0.3/EVENT_PLANNING_PRODUCTION_AND_OPERATIONAL_WORKFLOWS_DESIGN_v1.0.md), [FRS v1.0](../implementation-design/v0.3/FORMS_REGISTRATION_AND_SUBMISSION_STUDIO_DESIGN_v1.0.md), [HPG v1.0](../implementation-design/v0.3/HOSPITALITY_PROTOCOL_AND_GUEST_SERVICES_DESIGN_v1.0.md), [RAI v1.0](../implementation-design/v0.3/REPORTING_ANALYTICS_AND_INTELLIGENCE_STUDIO_DESIGN_v1.0.md) elaborate future scope-specific permissions, not new implicit grants. AES setup/readiness/presets cannot bypass domain authority; EPW separates plan/task/shift assignment, approval review and execution; FRS separates author/publisher/intake/reviewer/mapper and protected attachment access; HPG separates service requester/coordinator/supplier and restricted actionable fields; RAI separates dataset/read/field/aggregate, design, export, schedule and download rights. Cross-party scope and current grant/actor rechecks apply to every job, artifact, projection and mutation. PAC/OAC authority ceilings and no automatic confidential-data access remain. Review exact permission codes at scheduled implementation; no permission migration here. Approved additive scope only; retain existing requirements, accepted ADRs, Blueprint v1.2, PROJECT_STATE and the #104/#112 → #105–107 → #110/#111/#108 development sequence. No immediate implementation, unrelated closure gates, environment republication or Blueprint v1.3 consolidation. Final integrated acceptance remains Phase 9.

# Eventor MVP scope — v0.1

**Status:** accepted initial product scope; organization-specific and GHB policies remain subject to validation  
**Date:** 2026-11-10  
**Reference deployment:** Gazi Husrev-beg's Library (GHB), Sarajevo  
**Related:** [Issue #4](https://github.com/TeraflopsBH/eventor/issues/4), ADR 0004, ADR 0006

## 1. Product position

Eventor is one platform with two distinct but composable product capabilities:

1. **Venue booking and resource management** — a venue provider receives inquiries, prices/approves requests, books spaces/resources and delivers venue-side services.
2. **Event organization and operations** — an event organizer manages participants, invitations/RSVP, seating, check-in and event-day work.

A deployment may use either capability or both. A particular booking does not automatically become a full operational event. An organization profile is a default, not a rigid product edition. Capabilities can be activated per booking/event and task ownership is explicit.

For the GHB reference deployment, the safest MVP assumption is that GHB acts primarily as a **venue provider**. Its renter remains the event organizer unless GHB explicitly accepts an organizer/operations service. The booking workflow must be useful and complete without collecting the renter's guest list.

## 2. Recommended release boundary

### Release 1 — Venue booking and venue operations

This is the first production-capable GHB workflow.

#### Included

**Organization and access**
- Organization and venue-provider configuration.
- Staff authentication, organization membership, scoped roles/permissions and audit.
- Configurable approval authorities and staff assignments.

**Venue/resource registry**
- Venue, building, level, space and approved space revision.
- Space availability calendar and operational time blocks for setup, rehearsal, event and teardown.
- Venue-owned bookable resources: equipment, staff/services, ancillary spaces and count-based pools.
- Capacity and resource inventory must be approved and revisioned.
- Venue configuration is not hardcoded to GHB; GHB data is a tenant's configuration.

**Public inquiry**
- Public form with organization/venue branding.
- Configurable fields, options, localization, validation and published revisions.
- Simple request intake: requester/customer, contracting details where needed, actual event organizer contact where known, event title/type, preferred date/time/duration, requested space, expected attendance if needed for venue rules, requested equipment/services, rehearsal/setup/teardown and notes.
- No guest-level attendee list, invitation data, RSVP answers or admission information.
- No account required for initial inquiry; public endpoint has abuse controls and rate limits.

**Booking administration**
- Inquiry inbox, triage, clarifications and internal notes.
- Separate editable booking draft prepopulated from the inquiry.
- Original request remains immutable.
- Configurable offer, internal approval and organizer-acceptance steps.
- Explicit authorized confirmation with atomic space/resource reservation.
- Manual booking creation without a public inquiry.
- Customer/authorised organizer cancellation requests and venue-provider-initiated cancellation, with configurable review/approval, effective cancellation, commercial consequence recording and atomic resource release.
- Withdrawal, expiry, postponement/rescheduling and controlled amendment/change order remain distinct outcomes. Cancellation does not automatically create an operational event or cancel a linked organizer-owned event.
- Requested, approved and delivered resource/service values remain distinct.

**Commercial configuration**
- Versioned service/equipment catalogues and effective-dated price lists.
- Configurable duration/quantity/add-on/discount/surcharge/tax rules.
- Immutable quotation/offer snapshots.
- Prices and policies are organization-owned configuration. Historical GHB prices are not treated as current policy until confirmed.

**Venue fulfilment**
- Venue-side preparation/fulfilment tasks for booked resources and services.
- Rehearsal, setup and teardown schedule blocks.
- Venue-side status, issues and completion confirmation.
- Task ownership and assignment to venue staff/teams.
- Booking confirmation and operational communications by email through a provider abstraction.

**Operational foundation**
- Audit trail, notifications and background jobs.
- Booking/resource availability conflict protection at database and service layers.
- Backups, restore procedure, health checks and deployment runbook before production use.

#### Explicitly excluded from Release 1 by default

- Guest Registry and event attendee records.
- Guest invitation campaigns, personalized RSVP links and response history.
- Seating plans and guest-to-seat/zone allocation.
- Guest portal and guest-facing wayfinding.
- Admission QR credentials and check-in/attendance scanning.
- Organizer-side external protocol/permit coordination records.
- Full event-day organizer cockpit and guest/staff operational workspaces.
- Ticket sales/payment processing.
- Digital signatures and legal contract automation unless separately required.

These are not permanently excluded from Eventor. They are optional capabilities planned for later releases and may be enabled for a particular event when the relevant organization has responsibility and a clear use case.

### Release 2 — Organizer event workspace

Release 2 adds an operational event that can be created independently or linked to a confirmed venue booking.

- Organization-owned events/sessions and optional event capabilities.
- Persistent Guest Registry and event participation records.
- Event-specific imports, duplicate review and supervised merge.
- Invitation issuance/delivery and secure invitation-link lifecycle.
- Guest self-service and staff-recorded RSVP.
- RSVP deadlines, reminders and append-only response history.
- Booking-event linking under explicit cross-organization collaboration.
- Approved venue-space snapshots, event-owned allocation resources and provenance.
- Optional event responsibilities and external prerequisites.

The organizer can run this capability in its own organization. A venue provider sees only booking/venue information and explicitly shared task projections.

### Release 3 — Seating, admission and live operations

- SVG floor-plan editor and versioned event-space maps.
- Manual, category-based and solver-assisted seating/allocation.
- Hard/soft constraints, locks, proposals, diagnostics and human-approved commits.
- Guest-safe map and wayfinding projections.
- Admission QR credentials distinct from invitation links.
- Check-in PWA, attendance corrections and station management.
- Live Event Operations Cockpit and role-specific staff workspaces.
- Realtime outbox/WebSocket delivery, alerts, activity timeline and reports.

### Later capabilities

Offline check-in, advanced analytics, additional notification channels, expanded integrations, advanced scheduling/resource optimization and other capabilities can follow after the operational baseline is stable.

## 3. Core release-1 data boundary

A venue booking may store:
- Booking requester/customer identity and business contact.
- Contracting party and payer snapshots where required.
- Actual event organizer name/contact where supplied and needed for the venue contract.
- Event title/type, requested date/time/duration and expected attendance where relevant.
- Requested venue/services/resources, approved commitment, quote and delivery status.
- Venue-side operational notes and restricted commercial information.

It does **not** need:
- Attendee names and contact points.
- Invitation URLs/tokens or delivery history.
- RSVP answers or response notes.
- Individual seating assignments or guest category/relationship data.
- Admission QR credentials or check-in history.
- Organizer-only documents and external protocol details.

Collect additional information only when needed for a configured venue service or validated contractual/facility rule. The platform must distinguish a venue's operational need (for example expected aggregate attendance) from organizer event-management data.

## 4. Release-1 workflow acceptance scenarios

1. A visitor submits a venue inquiry without creating an account or supplying a guest list.
2. A booking administrator reviews the inquiry and creates a separate editable draft. Original inquiry values remain unchanged.
3. Staff map requested choices to approved venue resource/service lines; a form selection alone does not reserve inventory or create a charge.
4. The system calculates a quote from a published price revision; later price changes do not rewrite the issued offer.
5. An authorized approver issues/approves the offer and the organizer accepts if configured.
6. Confirmation atomically reserves all required spaces and resources. A conflict commits none of the booking/reservation changes.
7. Setup, rehearsal, event and teardown can occupy separately scheduled time blocks.
8. Venue staff fulfill only the venue-side tasks assigned to them; every important state change is auditable.
9. An authorised external booking contact can request cancellation without tenant membership; the request remains pending until any required venue approval is recorded.
10. The venue provider can initiate cancellation when it cannot provide a confirmed space/service, using configured authority and emergency-review rules.
11. Effective booking cancellation releases future reservations exactly once, records any policy-based commercial consequence and notifies configured booking contacts without overwriting the original confirmed snapshot.
12. A booking cancellation does not automatically cancel a linked operational event or expose its guest data.
13. The complete booking flow succeeds with no operational-event, event-guest, invitation, RSVP, allocation, credential or check-in records.
14. The booking's organizer/customer does not automatically receive a user account or tenant membership.
15. If an organizer later uses Eventor, a separate operational event can be explicitly linked through a scoped collaboration grant and immutable venue-space snapshot.
16. Guest, invitation, RSVP and organizer-only prerequisite data remain inaccessible to the venue provider unless a narrowly scoped task grant explicitly permits a required projection.

## 5. GHB validation gates

Before Release 1 is configured for production, GHB must confirm:
- Which rooms/spaces may be publicly rented and their approved capacities.
- Space/ancillary-room relationships and access limitations.
- Current equipment and service inventory and what is included in base rent.
- Current price list, taxes, discounts and weekend/holiday rules.
- Current opening/service hours, setup/rehearsal/teardown constraints and booking lead times.
- Who can prepare offers, approve discounts and confirm bookings.
- Who may submit booking cancellation requests, who at GHB may initiate venue-side cancellation, who approves/executes it, and which emergency exceptions apply.
- Confirmed cancellation notice periods, fees, deposits/credits/refunds and required customer notifications; do not enforce unconfirmed rules.
- Which information the venue legitimately needs from the organizer and how long it should be retained.
- Public form labels, options, mandatory fields and conditional behavior.
- Email sender/domain, reverse proxy/public hostname and data-retention policy.

Do not seed unconfirmed historical prices, capacities or protocols as enforced production rules.

## 6. Technical sequencing

1. Resolve accepted organization ownership, collaboration and database integrity designs (ADR 0006; Issues #12/#13).
2. Produce the first executable PostgreSQL migrations and validate them against a supported PostgreSQL version (Issue #2).
3. Complete OpenAPI v0.3 contract coverage and validation (Issues #3/#17).
4. Agree Release-1 role/permission matrix and approval authority, including booking cancellation authority ([Issue #21](https://github.com/TeraflopsBH/eventor/issues/21)).
5. Build foundation: auth, organization membership, configuration, audit, API contracts and test harness.
6. Build booking/resource workflows in vertical slices.
7. Run a GHB pilot using synthetic/demo data, then perform approved production onboarding.
8. Implement organizer event operations and guest capabilities as independently activatable follow-on releases.

The existing v0.2 backlog remains a source list; its phase labels need remapping to this release boundary after the MVP scope is approved.

# Public booking form field schema v1

This document defines the validation contract for the `field_schema` JSONB value stored on an immutable `booking_form_revisions` row and returned by the public booking-form projection.

## Versioning

A new published schema should include `"schemaVersion": 1`. Existing revisions that predate this contract and contain only `{"fields":[...]}` are interpreted as version 1. An explicit `null`, unknown version or unsupported field definition is invalid. Unknown future versions must not be interpreted as version 1.

The public submission API loads the exact revision identified by `formRevisionId`, verifies that it belongs to the requested active form and organization, and validates answers against that revision before encrypting or submitting them. A newer publication does not change an already published revision; a still-published older revision remains submit-capable. The database submission command rechecks that the same revision is still published immediately before creating the inquiry.

## Schema shape

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "fields": [
    {
      "code": "event_date",
      "type": "date",
      "label": "Requested event date",
      "required": true
    },
    {
      "code": "event_name",
      "type": "text",
      "label": "Event name",
      "required": true,
      "minLength": 2,
      "maxLength": 120
    },
    {
      "code": "estimated_guests",
      "type": "number",
      "label": "Estimated guests",
      "required": true,
      "integer": true,
      "min": 1,
      "max": 5000
    },
    {
      "code": "room_layout",
      "type": "select",
      "label": "Preferred room layout",
      "required": true,
      "options": [
        { "value": "theatre", "label": "Theatre" },
        { "value": "banquet", "label": "Banquet" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "code": "equipment",
      "type": "multiselect",
      "label": "Requested equipment",
      "required": false,
      "minItems": 0,
      "maxItems": 2,
      "options": [
        { "value": "projector", "label": "Projector" },
        { "value": "microphone", "label": "Microphone" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "code": "accept_terms",
      "type": "checkbox",
      "label": "I accept the stated terms",
      "required": true
    }
  ]
}
```

Each field has a unique `code` matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,79}$`. A schema may contain at most 100 fields. `required` defaults to false. Labels and descriptive presentation properties do not change validation behavior.

## Supported field types

| Type | Submitted JSON value | Validation |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | string | `minLength` / `maxLength`; default maximum 5,000 characters |
| `textarea` | string | Same string-length rules as `text` |
| `email` | string | String-length rules plus a basic email-address format check |
| `phone` | string | 3–50 characters, digits and common international phone punctuation only |
| `number` | JSON number | Finite number; optional `min`, `max`, and `integer: true` constraints |
| `date` | string | Real calendar date in `YYYY-MM-DD` format |
| `datetime` | string | ISO date-time with an explicit `Z` or numeric UTC offset |
| `time` | string | 24-hour `HH:mm` or `HH:mm:ss` |
| `select` | string | Must exactly match one configured option value |
| `multiselect` | array of strings | Every value must match an option; duplicates are rejected; optional `minItems` / `maxItems` apply |
| `checkbox` | boolean | Must be a JSON boolean; a required checkbox must be `true` |

For `select` and `multiselect`, `options` is a non-empty array of unique objects with non-empty `value` and `label` strings (each at most 200 characters). Those values are part of the immutable form revision and are the accepted answer values.

String fields may define integer `minLength` and `maxLength` values from 0 through 5,000, with `maxLength` at least 1 and not less than `minLength`. Numeric `min` and `max` must be finite and `min` cannot exceed `max`. `integer` is valid only for number fields. Multi-select item bounds must be integers within the number of configured options and `minItems` cannot exceed `maxItems`.

## Answer semantics

The `answers` object is keyed by field `code`. Unknown keys are rejected rather than silently stored. Every required field must have a value. For any field, `null`, an empty string (including whitespace-only text) and an omitted property are treated as unanswered. An optional field may be omitted; a required field may not. An empty array is a submitted multiselect value and is checked against `minItems` / `maxItems`; it does not bypass those bounds. Arrays supplied to any non-multiselect field are rejected as a type mismatch. A required multiselect must contain at least one selected value. A required checkbox is only satisfied by `true`; `false` is an explicit negative answer and does not satisfy a required acknowledgement.

Optional fields may be omitted. If a value is supplied, it must match the declared JSON type and every constraint for that field. Numeric strings are not numbers. Choice answers must use the option values from the exact submitted revision; labels are not accepted in place of values.

## Enforcement and boundaries

Validation runs in the Fastify public inquiry route after the exact revision projection is loaded and before ECP1 encryption and the database submission command. Invalid answers return HTTP 422 and do not consume an inquiry rate-limit slot. A malformed or unsupported published schema fails closed with HTTP 500 and is not accepted as valid input.

The database stores the full submitted answer object encrypted with the tenant-bound ECP1 contact codec. The database cannot inspect those ciphertext values; callers must use the API boundary rather than invoking the privileged submission function outside the trusted application.

The v1 public projection currently supports options embedded directly in `field_schema`. Catalogue-bound option expansion, conditional visibility/dependency rules, file-upload fields and attachments are not part of v1. Non-empty attachment references continue to receive HTTP 422 until a separate authorized, malware-scanned upload workflow is implemented.

# Self-hosted deployment and operations runbook

**Status:** deployment procedure draft; not a production certification.  
**Scope:** the current Fastify API, notification worker, Vue staff web and PostgreSQL database. This runbook deliberately separates repository-verifiable steps from environment-specific operational controls that have not yet been exercised.

## 1. Deployment status and prerequisites

The accepted deployment decision is self-hosted Linux. Docker and managed cloud services are not mandatory. The repository currently provides application build/start commands, PostgreSQL role bootstrap and a checksum-verified migration runner. It does **not** yet provide a complete tested systemd unit set, reverse-proxy configuration, automated backup/restore tooling or a production recovery drill.

Before a first deployment, prepare:

- A supported Linux host and a supported Node.js 22 release (staff-web development documentation specifies Node 22.16.0; use the same pinned release for reproducible builds).
- PostgreSQL 18.6, reachable only from the API/worker hosts and authorized administration/migration hosts.
- A trusted TLS certificate authority for PostgreSQL connections; production connection strings must use `sslmode=verify-full`.
- A same-origin HTTPS reverse proxy for the staff web and API. Preserve the `/api` prefix mapping expected by the staff web, or configure `VITE_API_BASE_URL` consistently at build time.
- Separate secret/configuration storage for API, worker and database credentials. Do not commit real environment files.
- A backup destination independent of the database host, with access controls and encryption appropriate for guest/contact data.
- An operator-approved maintenance and recovery window. No zero-downtime migration guarantee is currently documented.

Do not treat this draft runbook as evidence that a target host, firewall, proxy, certificate, backup schedule or recovery objective has been tested.

## 2. Process and network topology

Recommended initial topology:

- Reverse proxy: public HTTPS entry point; route the staff-web application and `/api/*` to the API after removing the `/api` prefix.
- API: Fastify process listening on the configured `HOST`/`PORT` (defaults to `0.0.0.0:8080`, which binds all interfaces). Set `HOST` to a private interface address (or loopback when the proxy is local) where practical, and enforce firewall rules so the API port is never directly reachable from the public internet.
- Notification worker: separate process using only `EVENTOR_WORKER_DATABASE_URL`.
- PostgreSQL: private network only. The API uses separate runtime and auth pools; the worker uses its own worker role.
- Staff web: build the static application and serve its generated assets through the reverse proxy. The Vite development server and `vite preview` are not production servers.

Only expose the reverse proxy publicly. Restrict database ingress to the required hosts and administration network. If the API is behind a proxy, set `EVENTOR_TRUST_PROXY_CIDRS` to the exact proxy addresses/CIDRs; never trust arbitrary forwarded headers.

## 3. Database initialization and migration

Perform this on a new or explicitly approved target database, using a database administrator account for role bootstrap:

1. Create the Eventor database using the organization's approved encoding, locale, ownership and storage policy.
2. Bootstrap the least-privilege roles from the repository root:

   ```sh
   psql "$ADMIN_DATABASE_URL" -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \
     -v database_name=eventor -f scripts/db/bootstrap-roles.sql
   ```

   Connect `ADMIN_DATABASE_URL` directly to the Eventor database; the bootstrap script does not switch databases. The script reconciles role attributes and memberships. It does not set passwords.
3. Set distinct strong passwords for `eventor_migrator`, `eventor_runtime`, `eventor_auth` and `eventor_worker` using the organization's secret-management process or interactive PostgreSQL `\password`. Never place passwords in shell history or commit them.
4. Verify the role attributes and membership graph using `tests/database/auth_role_smoke.sql` and the role checks in the database CI workflow, adapted only as needed for the target environment.
5. Take and verify a pre-migration backup using the organization's PostgreSQL backup procedure.
6. Run migrations from a trusted release checkout, connecting as `eventor_migrator`:

   ```sh
   cd apps/api
   npm ci
   npm run build
   cd ../..
   DATABASE_URL="$EVENTOR_MIGRATOR_DATABASE_URL" scripts/db/migrate.sh
   ```

   `EVENTOR_MIGRATOR_DATABASE_URL` is a shell variable supplied by the deployment secret store; it must connect as `eventor_migrator`. The migration runner requires `psql`, `sha256sum`, PostgreSQL 18.6 and the repository migration directory. It verifies checksums, serializes concurrent migration attempts and records each migration in the same transaction as its schema changes.
7. Run the database smoke/security tests against a disposable or explicitly approved test database before production traffic. Do not run destructive test fixtures against production.

Migrations are forward-only. There is no automatic down-migration command. A checksum mismatch on an already-applied migration is a stop condition: do not edit the historical migration or bypass the check.

## 4. Build and configure application processes

Build from the same reviewed release commit that was migrated:

```sh
cd apps/api
npm ci
npm run build

cd ../staff-web
npm ci
VITE_API_BASE_URL=/api npm run build
```

The staff-web build produces static assets in its Vite output directory. Publish those assets to the configured web root using an atomic release/symlink strategy chosen by the operator. Keep the API and staff-web assets on compatible release versions.

Configure the API process with:

- `EVENTOR_RUNTIME_DATABASE_URL`
- `EVENTOR_AUTH_DATABASE_URL`
- `EVENTOR_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`
- `EVENTOR_AUTH_FINGERPRINT_KEY`
- `EVENTOR_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY`
- `EVENTOR_CONTACT_ENCRYPTION_KEY`
- `EVENTOR_DELIVERY_CREDENTIALS_KEY`
- `EVENTOR_PUBLIC_INQUIRY_FINGERPRINT_KEY`
- `EVENTOR_BOOKING_CAPABILITY_KEY`

The worker process requires:

- `EVENTOR_WORKER_DATABASE_URL`
- `EVENTOR_CONTACT_ENCRYPTION_KEY`
- `EVENTOR_DELIVERY_CREDENTIALS_KEY`

Booking-offer and guest-invitation email delivery additionally require worker-only `EVENTOR_PUBLIC_APP_BASE_URL`; set it to the HTTPS public web-app base URL (including any deployment path prefix) so invitation links resolve to the guest portal. Provider callback URL display requires API-side `EVENTOR_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL`. Optional pool and worker tuning variables are documented in `apps/api/.env.example`.

Generate six independent cryptographically random 32-byte keys and base64-encode each one. Never reuse a key across purposes or place keys in source control, command-line arguments, logs or deployment artifacts. Keep the booking-capability key stable while issued links remain valid. Encryption-key rotation requires an explicit re-encryption procedure; replacing a key alone makes existing ciphertext unreadable.

Set `EVENTOR_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` to the exact HTTPS staff-web origin(s), not a wildcard. Configure API and worker database URLs with certificate and hostname verification. Use separate OS service accounts with only the filesystem and network permissions each process needs. Run the API and worker as separate supervised services; do not run either as root or with migration/owner credentials.

The repository now includes example systemd units and installation guidance in `deploy/systemd/`. They are templates, not target-host-validated service definitions: confirm the Node executable path, service accounts, release symlink, environment-file permissions, sandbox compatibility, restart policy and graceful-shutdown timeout on the selected distribution. A tested reverse-proxy configuration is still not included; configure and review that separately before deployment.

## 5. First-start verification

Before opening public traffic, verify all of the following:

- API and worker start under their dedicated service accounts and remain healthy after a controlled restart.
- API runtime/auth and worker connections authenticate as the intended PostgreSQL roles; none uses `eventor_owner` or `eventor_migrator`.
- PostgreSQL connections validate the server certificate and hostname.
- Staff web and API are served over the same HTTPS origin; cookies retain the required `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite` and `__Host-` behavior.
- The exact staff-web origin is allow-listed; untrusted origins and untrusted forwarded headers are rejected.
- A controlled staff login/logout works, CSRF checks reject missing/invalid tokens, and tenant boundaries are verified.
- Worker queue processing is observed using synthetic test data and a controlled test mailbox. Do not send production campaigns as a deployment smoke test.
- Logs and metrics are collected without session tokens, passwords, encryption keys, guest contact values, ciphertext or provider secrets.
- Public endpoints, rate limits, firewall rules, DNS and TLS renewal have been reviewed.

A passing application health check alone does not establish that email delivery, backup recovery or all business workflows are production-ready.

### Guest invitation SMTP ambiguity and recovery

Guest invitation email delivery is **at-most-once after an ambiguous SMTP submission**, not exactly-once. A worker records an attempt as `uncertain` when SMTP may have accepted the message but the worker cannot establish the outcome. The same conservative transition is used when a worker lease expires while the delivery is `sending`. Neither case is automatically retried. This avoids silently sending duplicate personal invitation links.

For an uncertain invitation:

1. Open the invitation's delivery-attempt history in the staff workspace. Record the attempt time, failure code, attempt number and any provider message reference shown there. The history is diagnostic; it does not prove inbox delivery.
2. Have an operator with access to the configured SMTP provider's message/activity logs check the relevant submission window and recipient. Use the provider's accepted/rejected result, not merely a successful TCP connection or SMTP authentication. Do not copy recipient addresses, invitation URLs, bearer tokens or provider credentials into tickets or application logs.
3. If the provider confirms acceptance, do not reissue just to clear the uncertain status. The current application has no provider callback/reconciliation path that can safely convert an uncertain guest-invitation attempt to delivered/sent; retain the uncertain audit record and handle guest communication through the approved support process.
4. If the provider definitively confirms that it did not accept the message, an authorized organizer may reissue the invitation. Reissue rotates the capability and invalidates the previous link; verify the guest's contact readiness and explain that only the newest link is valid.
5. If the provider cannot determine the outcome, leave the delivery uncertain. Do not manually change its status, reset its attempt count, delete attempt history, or requeue it. Reissuing in this situation can produce duplicate emails and invalidate a link that may already have reached the guest.

**Current limitation:** guest-invitation delivery does not yet have a provider webhook or operator reconciliation command. The attempt history retains a provider reference for confirmed SMTP success, but an ambiguous submission/expired lease may have no usable provider reference. Provider-side investigation may therefore require a tightly controlled search by recipient and approximate submission time. This limitation must be resolved before claiming automated recovery or exactly-once delivery. CI uses fake SMTP and does not validate provider-side lookup behavior.

## 6. Backup, restore and recovery requirements

A production operator must select and document a PostgreSQL backup method before accepting real data. The repository does not prescribe a tested backup implementation yet.

At minimum, the operational design must specify:

- Backup type and cadence (base backups and, if required, continuous WAL archiving/PITR).
- Encryption in transit and at rest, separate storage credentials and off-host/off-site retention.
- Retention periods, deletion policy and access audit.
- Monitoring for failed, incomplete, late or unexpectedly small backups and WAL archive gaps.
- Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO), approved by the organization.
- A restore procedure for a clean host, including PostgreSQL configuration, role/bootstrap state, database restore, application release, secret restoration and DNS/proxy cutover.
- Protection and recoverability of the six application encryption keys. A database backup without the matching keys is insufficient to recover encrypted contact, inquiry, delivery or offer data.
- A recurring restore drill in an isolated environment, with documented timings and integrity checks.

Before every production migration or release that changes database behavior, take a verified backup and confirm that the recovery path is available. If a migration fails, stop deployment and preserve logs. Do not improvise manual schema edits or assume a down migration exists. Recovery options are a tested backup/PITR restore or a reviewed forward-fix migration; choose according to the incident and the organization's data-loss tolerance.

## 7. Upgrade and rollback procedure

1. Review the release commit, migration list, dependency changes and CI results. Confirm that the exact commit to deploy is the one validated.
2. Confirm a tested backup/restore path and available encryption keys.
3. Put the application into an operator-controlled maintenance state if required. The current repository does not provide a complete maintenance-mode switch; coordinate traffic and worker shutdown explicitly.
4. Stop or pause worker processing and prevent concurrent migration runners.
5. Apply migrations once, using the dedicated migrator connection.
6. Deploy the API and staff-web assets from the same release commit.
7. Start the API, verify authentication and tenant-scoped read paths, then start the worker and verify queue processing.
8. Re-enable traffic and monitor application/database errors, queue age, SMTP outcomes, disk capacity and backup status.
9. If application rollback is required after a schema change, do not automatically restore old application code against the new schema. Confirm backward compatibility first. If the database must be restored, follow the tested recovery procedure and explicitly account for writes made after the backup/PITR point.

No prior released production schema baseline has been established in this repository. Upgrade-from-previous-release compatibility is therefore unverified and must be tested once a real release baseline exists.

## 8. Production readiness evidence still required

The following are external or unimplemented gates, not claims that this repository can satisfy by itself:

- Tested target-host installation and service supervision.
- Reviewed production reverse-proxy and firewall configuration.
- Secret provisioning, access control, backup and key-recovery procedures.
- Automated backup monitoring and a successful isolated restore/PITR drill.
- Approved RPO/RTO and incident ownership.
- Upgrade test from a defined preceding release schema.
- Load, capacity, log-retention and operational monitoring baselines.
- A documented security/incident response process.

Until these are evidenced, classify the deployment as **pre-production**.

## 9. External acceptance evidence

Use `docs/operations/EXTERNAL_ACCEPTANCE_EVIDENCE.md` as the dated evidence record for browser-driven business workflow acceptance, Resend/SMTP sandbox acceptance, prior-schema migration upgrade rehearsal, backup/restore/PITR drills and target-host/network acceptance. Assign an accountable owner and exact candidate SHA to each activity. Mark activities deferred until the required isolated environment, credentials, representative data or approved operational targets exist; do not convert missing evidence into a pass. Production remains blocked until the required evidence and approvals are complete.

# Remote acceptance and verification boundaries

This document distinguishes repeatable GitHub-hosted checks from acceptance that requires a real, separately approved environment. CI is not production certification.

## Automated on the integration branch

The `Contracts and PostgreSQL migrations` workflow runs:

- OpenAPI 3.1 validation/lint, API route tests, TypeScript generation/type-checking and high/critical dependency audit.
- Staff-web regression tests, type-check/build and dependency audit.
- PostgreSQL 18.6 fresh migration chain, migration-history-gap guard, populated 000073-to-000074 upgrade rehearsal, RLS/tenant isolation, authorization/revocation races and concurrency regressions.
- PostgreSQL-backed session authentication, worker/fake-SMTP integration, booking/commercial end-to-end tests and migration 000114 draft reservation-release behavior.
- systemd unit syntax and referenced identity checks.
- A logical `pg_dump`/restore rehearsal into a separate ephemeral database, including comparison of selected row counts and verification that the restored migration-000114 function exists.
- Full reachable Git-history secret scanning in the separate secret-history workflow.

The logical backup/restore check validates a dump and restore in ephemeral CI. It does not exercise WAL archiving, point-in-time recovery, off-host retention, encryption-key escrow, or recovery objectives.

## Optional external probes

The `Optional external acceptance probes` workflow can be enabled without placing credentials in source control:

- Set repository variable `EVENTOR_SMTP_SANDBOX_ENABLED=true` and configure the `EVENTOR_SMTP_*` repository secrets to run one explicit test message through the configured non-production SMTP sandbox.
- Set repository variable `EVENTOR_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` to an approved public HTTPS endpoint to check certificate validation, successful HTTP response, HSTS, `X-Content-Type-Options` and `Referrer-Policy`.

These probes are opt-in. A skipped job is not a pass. The SMTP probe verifies provider acceptance of the configured test recipient; it does not prove inbox placement, bounce/complaint processing or domain reputation.

## Not established by ephemeral CI

The following still require an identified, isolated acceptance environment and accountable operator:

- Full browser-driven business workflows through the deployed staff web and public booking pages. API session integration is not equivalent to browser acceptance.
- Real Resend/SMTP sandbox acceptance unless the optional job is explicitly enabled and succeeds.
- Upgrade from a representative prior deployed database snapshot. The current 000073-to-000074 rehearsal is a targeted synthetic upgrade, not evidence of an actual customer or production baseline.
- Backup destination, off-host retention, encryption-key recovery and WAL/PITR restore drill against an approved RPO/RTO.
- Target Linux host service startup, filesystem permissions, firewall, reverse proxy, trusted-proxy CIDRs, DNS, TLS renewal, PostgreSQL TLS and operational monitoring.
- Product/venue acceptance, security review and production release approval.

Never point repository CI at a production database or production mail recipients. Use synthetic data and separately approved staging credentials. Record the exact candidate commit SHA and sanitized evidence for each external activity. Missing evidence remains deferred, not passed.

# External deployment acceptance evidence

**Disposition:** blocked / not yet executed  
**Candidate:** record the exact reviewed Git commit SHA for every activity.  
**Safety:** use isolated, non-production infrastructure and synthetic data only. Do not use production recipients, production credentials or production databases for acceptance.

This record is intentionally a template. Empty fields are not evidence of a pass.

## Repository CI boundary

The integration branch's `docs/operations/REMOTE_ACCEPTANCE.md` records the checks available in GitHub-hosted CI. CI now includes an isolated logical PostgreSQL dump/restore rehearsal and provides opt-in SMTP sandbox and public HTTPS probes. These checks do not establish a production backup/PITR drill, full browser business acceptance, a real deployed-database upgrade, or target-host/network acceptance. A skipped optional probe is not a pass. Record the exact candidate SHA and sanitized run evidence when an external activity is actually completed.
